maintopic: REPRESENTATION OF THE NORTHWEST TERRITORIES IN THE SENATE.

speechtext:
The MINISTER OF JUSTICE (Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick) moved the first reading of Bill (No. 253) to increase the representation of the North-west Territories in the Senate. He said : Hon. gentlemen are aware that, under the British North America Amendment Act of 1886, it is provided that the parliament of Canada may, from time to time, make provision for the representation in the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, or either of them, of any territory for the time being formed in the Dominion of Canada, but not included in any of the provinces thereof. In the following year a Bill was introduced, which appears as chapter 3 of the statute of 1887, by which provision was made for the re-Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
presentation of the North-west Territories in the Senate by two members. Since that time the population has materially increased. The population of the organized part, Assiniboia, Alberta and Saskatchewan, which was only 25,515 in 1881, increased to 66,799 in 1891, and to 159,940 in 1901. Of course, since then there has been even a greater proportion of increase. _ The increase in the unorganized territory was from 30,931 in 1881 to 52,709 in 1901. Taking these two together and allowing for increase since 1901, the proportion of representation of the territories in the Senate will be about the same as it is in Ontario.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

maintopic: YUKON TERRITORY ACT AMENDMENT.

speechtext:
The MINISTER OF JUSTICE (Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 254) further to amend the Yukon Territory Act. He said : This Bill is introduced merely for the purpose of setting at rest a doubt that was expressed by the Supreme Court at its last sitting with regard to the Court of Appeal for the Yukon. They expressed doubt as to whether or not, under the statute as we have it, two judges of the Court of Appeal form a quorum of that court. It would seem to me, as a matter of course, that in a court of three judges two would form a quorum. However, the Supreme Court expressed doubt on that point, and this is to set that doubt at rest,	1
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I would like to know upon what principle the subdivision of the city of Toronto is made ? Every recognized rule supposed to govern a matter of this kind is completely ignored. Take the case of South Toronto, where the hon. gentlemen have succeeded in carving out a constituency where they hope to get a majority of 150. They have done that by taking a strip about 400 yards wide running from near the Humber bridge down to the Don bridge. They have taken a piece here and there off each of the other constituencies. It is the most extraordinary looking constituency that can be found in the Dominion of Canada. I would like to know why they departed from the recognized boundaries of the constituencies heretofore existing, from the boundaries of the ridings, from concession lines, and from every other landmark in making this division ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I cannot understand the hon. member for Toronto in asserting that there is any difference in dealing with the county of York from the rule followed elsewhere. My hon. friend knows that this matter was referred to the committee. In the last redistribution almost every other one of the great counties of Ontario had been cut up, and parts taken from one county and added to another, or some constituencies were in three or four counties. My hon. friend knows that, and he knows that they had left parts of the municipality of Toronto in the county of York. He knows that when this matter was referred to the special committee, the principle of county boundaries was adopted. There has been no variation from that rule except by agreement. Then we were bound to take the population of the city of Toronto as it was within its municipal boundaries.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: But the hon. gentleman has not answered my question as to why such a scandalous division has been made.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend knows that there were two plans of division submitted to the committee. The members of the committee could have but little knowledge of the local conditions in a large city like Toronto. Plans were prepared, and the members for Toronto, as I understand, handed in a proposition. I will ask the hon. gentleman who is familiar with the local conditions, to point out wherein every principal that was adopted by the committee as ruling principles was not violated in the proposition submitted by himself and his colleagues. I asked him to explain that when it was before the committee. Now we are
getting accustomed to hear the hon. gentleman and his friends get up in the House and talk about these scandalous transactions, without any evidence whatever. I am surprised to hear my hon. friend from West Toronto using language of that kind. We had before us two propositions submitted to the committee for consideration. They were compared, and I would like the hon. gentleman to point out where the proposition adopted by the committee has less merit than the one he and his colleagues submitted.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Of course we all know that the hon. gentleman is simply bluffing, if that is a parliamentary term. He has not attempted to answer a plain question. The subdivision of South Toronto is indefensible, and nobody knows it better than the hon. gentleman and those who are associated with him. To take a strip of territory 400 yards wide and six miles long and constitute it one division of a city-I say no more indefensible proposition was ever made to any community. There is no community of interest between the extreme east and the extreme west of the city, there is no compactness in the division. The division was made for the sole and only purpose of trying to get a liberal representative. If, according to our proposition, the territory east of Yonge street were given two members, and1 the territory west of Spadina avenue were given two members all classes of the citizens would be represented, the industrial classes, the manufacturing classes, the commercial and professional classes.	I ask those gentlemen why in subdividing the city of Toronto, they have taken a strip from the extreme western limit at the Humber about 400 yards wide in some places, and fifty yards wide in others, a strip running along the front of the city, and constituted that into a constituency ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman said I was bluffing, and! he had a splendid opportunity to have called that bluff, and to have shown it to the committee. I told the hon. gentleman that there were two propositions before this committee, and let the hon. gentleman, instead of imputing motives to the members of the committee, point out any principle that is violated in this proposition that was not violated previously. He ought to be more familiar with the local conditions than the members of the committee. Let him go back and show where there is any principle violated in this that was not violated in the last readjustment of that constituency as it now exists. Take it backwards or forwards. I am prepared to take him on his own proposition, and I ask him to show, as between the two propositions, that there has not been in this one a more evident attachment to principle and to the rules that ought to govern a redistribution

of seats in a city, tlian was shown in the last redistribution.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I am asking the hon. gentleman to show the difference, I am asking for information.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman wants to discuss it seriously, I will give my views in regard to it, and I will leave it to the judgment of the committee as to whether I am right or not. The municipality of Toronto has to be divided into five constituencies. By adhering as nearly as possible to a community of interest and to a fair division of a city, we find that the populations of the various divisions are as follows :
South Toronto	 38,205

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
The hon. gentlemen opposite, instead of getting up and moving an amendment to any portion of this Bill which does not suit them, get up and say : This was done for political or partisan motives. Let any hon. member of this House take the two propositions and compare them, and let him judge as to whether those who made the division of the city of Toronto, dividing it into five equal constituencies, were influenced by political motives as much as those who made the propoposition in amendment which violates every rule that could apply to a fair redistribution. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) proposes to have one constituency with two members. What is the reason for that ? There is no rule that I can understand that applies to it. On the contrary, that principle would never be adopted unless for some good and sufficient reason.
Therefore, the rule requiring the equalization of population which would govern the committee in making a division of this kind has been adhered to ns nearly as possible. In a city like Toronto, with a large population, this is almost an equal division of the population. Then, as to the complaint which has been made, and as to the proposition which has been submitted by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke), I will leave it to the committee to say if the divisions as embodied in the Bill are not compact in form, and if they do not carry out the rule as to the community of interest. I will tell the hon. gentleman why his proposition is a worse one than that which is embodied in the Bill. In the first place, the hon. gentleman, for some reason or other, puts two constituencies into one. If the hon. gentleman had made a proposition to avoid an inequality of population or to conform to wards or other municipal divisions, indefensible as it might be in some respects, he would have applied1 some-principle to his proposition that might have influenced the committee. What principle was there in his proposition? For some reason, I do not know what, it appeared to him and the other members from Toronto that it would- be better, instead of making equal and fair divisions as we are making and to have one member for every constituency, to have one constituency represented by two members.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Why not?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I said on one occasion that I thought perhaps these hon. gentlemen were influenced by political motives in making this proposition.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Do you charge us with being influenced by political motives?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: We have been charged with that every minute of the day.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: What is that ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I will leave it to my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) to say why this rule was suggested. In every possible way the amendment violates all the rules that might govern the committee to a much greater extent than has been done in the proposition embodied in the Bill.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: If I understand what the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) has said, I think it is that the principle of adopting two members for one constituency is a bad one.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) knows my views in regard to that. I did not use the word ' bad.' I said that unless there was some special and sufficient reason for it, it was not a good rule to adopt.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: What is the special reason that induced the committee to apply this rule to Ottawa, Halifax, Queen's, P.E.I., and St. John ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The simple reason is that the hon. gentleman did not propose to change the conditions existing there.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: That is a very satisfactory reason, no doubt. My hon. friend was controlled, I suppose, by the minority of the committee in that regard.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I have been to a great extent in this whole matter, probably.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: It is a pity that my hon. friend had not been ruled by the minority of the committee in other regards, because if he had been, we would have had a great deal less discussion. [DOT]

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Not a pity, I think.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Is that the only argument that can be made to show that we have made an unfair division of the city of Toronto ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: What is the only argument ? I aslc the hon. gentleman why he has followed that principle in four different cases, and the only answer he gives justifying his position, which ought to be based on some principle, is that the opposition did not offer any amendment.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I am prepared to give the bon. gentleman my answer if he thinks it necessary that we should discuss it again.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I had supposed that the hon. gentleman had based his redistribution of the province of Ontario, as well as of the whole Dominion, upon some principle. That is the claim that has been made. I would* like to know what principle it is which makes two members for a constituency all right in Ottawa, all right in Queen's, P.E.I., all right in Halifax, all right in St. John, and absolutely wrong in Toronto ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I did not say it was absolutely wrong. If the hon. gentleman had paid any attention to my language, he would have known that I did say that there might be special reasons why it would meet with the approval of the House and a majority of the committee.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: What special reasons are there in this case ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I will tell the committee some of the reasons in a minute.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) is at perfect liberty to explain why he thinks that condition should exist in Halifax, St. John, Ottawa, and the other constituency that he mentioned. When these constituencies are under consideration, I shall be glad to give my views as to why in these special cases they should be allowed to remain as they are, and why that rule was adopted. No reasons have been shown that I have ever heard why it would be better to apply that rule to the particular case of the city of Toronto, or why we should adopt the plan which has been submitted by the opposition rather than the plan which is recommended in this Bill.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The right hon. Prime Minister laid down the rule that municipal boundaries should be adhered to. In the past the constituencies of the city of Toronto have adhered to that principle to a very considerable extent.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: So we have here.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Almost entirely so, I am informed by my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke). The ward boundaries have been adhered to.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Do I understand that in the proposed amendment the ward boundaries are adhered to ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Not in the present proposition.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The city of Toronto is a city of very great length and of no very great width. It is several miles long -and about two and a half miles wide. The wards of Toronto are divided from north to south, as they should be. They are not divided from east to west to any extent. The lines runs north, and the constituencies in the past have been divided in that way.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that the proposition as embodied in the proposed amendment the lines are running north and south ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: 1 will deal with the amendment fully later on. I want to ask first : Why every rule laid down by the Prime Minister has been ignored in reference to Toronto. Neither concession lines, nor municipal boundaries, nor anything else iu that direction has been adhered to. It is a most remarkable thing that you should propose to divide Toronto, from east to west. South Toronto on this map looks so narrow that I wonder a man can walk through it from one end to the other without falling into the bay. It is a narrow strip a few hundred yards wide and five miles long. There is nothing compact about it ; there is no community of interest recognized in it, and it crosses the ward boundaries from one end to the other. I may reply to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hyman), that the proposition in the amendment is to divide Toronto in accordance with the principle laid down by the Prime Minister, by the ward boundaries from north to south; and the old concession line on Yonge street

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: But the line does not run all the way from north to south.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
What I was saying, when interrupted, was that Yonge street, the old concession line, the most important thoroughfare in Ontario running into the county of York sixty miles, is the dividing line according to the amendment, between east and centre Toronto. The next most important thoroughfare, Spadina avenue, running from north to south, is to be the division between Centre Toronto and West Toronto. West Toronto would have two members, and the only change necessary was to give one extra member to East Toronto, and thus you adhere to the municipal division of Toronto. That is. of course, assuming that Toronto would only get five members. I cannot understand what rule

guided the committee in making the division of Toronto as they have done. According to our views, we think Toronto should have equal representation with other parts of Ontario which would have given us eight members, but even suppose we only got me extra member, which we should have on every principle of justice, then we would have had one member for each of the six wards, and the municipal boundaries would have been adhered to.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I understand the hon. member to say that the amendment proposes that Yonge street should be the dividing line between East and Centre Toronto. The hon. gentleman may be right, but the map which I have in front of me shows that Yonge street has only been used as that division line to a certain extent. It leaves out a certain portion of North Toronto which if the Yonge street line were continued all the way up, would have put it in East Toronto.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: We adhered to the concession line.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The statement made was that the Yonge street division line was adhered to from north to south, and as we have been asked our reasons for the proposed division of Toronto, I should like to have the reasons from the other side as to why that line was not adhered to right through.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: That's easy.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I suppose it is. I could ascribe reasons myself if I wished to. We are told that South Toronto is a long narrow strip, but we have the advantage of having here not only a map of the proposed redistribution under the Bill, but a map of the redistribution of 1892, as well as of the division proposed in the amendment of gentlemen opposite. If any hon. gentler man .will look at the map of East Toronto represented by my hon. friend (Mr. Kemp) he will find that it is much narrower than the present proposed South Toronto, and he will find that it is not nearly as shapely in any way as the division of East Toronto proposed in the Bill.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: And the hon. gentleman (Mr. Kemp) has not fallen into the bay yet.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Let us examine for a moment the population of the different divisions under the two propositions. Under the Bill South Toronto has a unit of 38,205 ; East Toronto, 39,529 ; North Toronto. 41,434 ; Centre Toronto, 43,861, and West Toronto, 44,991. It will be noticed that the difference in the unit between the largest and the smallest of these constituencies is 6,786. Now under the Bill of 1891, the unit of the existing constituencies in Toronto is as follows :	Centre Toronto. 26.632 ;
West Toronto 36,913 ; East Toronto, 43,564.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: It will be noticed here that the difference between the largest and the smallest Toronto constituency at present is 16,932, as against 6,786 in the present Bill.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The amendment contained no such discrepancy as that.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I am comparing the division in 1892 which the hon. gentlemen opposite are responsible for, with the proposition which is now before this House, and that is a fair eomjDarison.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: No one says it isn't.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
We have now before us two propositions in regard to the city of Toronto, the one in the Bill and the one in the amendment. Under the amendment they propose that they shall take the eastern part of the city of Toronto with a population of 82,044, and give it two members. Then they propose that they shall take one constituency out of the centre, although they do not run the dividing line for the whole way, and make a constituency of 36,347. Then they propose to take the whole of West Toronto, with a population of 89,649, and give it two members. According to the proposition in the Bill the largest unit is West Toronto, 44,991, and the smallest South Toronto, 38,205, making a difference of only 6,786. According to that proposition of hon. gentlemen opposite West Toronto would be the largest unit with 48,824, and Centre Toronto the smallest with 36,347, a difference of 8,477. or 1,700 more than is proposed by the Bill. It is quite true that the proposition in the Bill does to some extent break ward boundaries, but it is just as true that the proposition handed in by gentlemen opposite breaks ward boundaries also. There is no difference in the two propositions so far as that is concerned. Taking everything into consideration, I think the proposition of the committee compares very favourably with that of the amendment. ' *
Mi'. KEMP. The hon. gentleman asked why the line was run westward along Bloor street to Spadina avenue. There was only one reason for that: it was in order to give sufficient population to East Toronto. Spadina avenue is made the boundary line between West Toronto and Centre Toronto, as far north as Bloor street, and between West Toronto and East Toronto north of Bloor street. The hon. gentleman has given the figures of population which he applies to the three constituencies named in the amendment. I may say that we went over this matter very carefully. Our own estimates were not relied upon as to the population in these various constituencies, but we got the assistance of the officials in the city of Toronto. The population of the constituencies as proposed in the amendment are given by the hon. gentleman as follows : West Toronto, 89,649 ; Centre Toronto, 36,-

347 ; East Toronto, 82,044. Our figures, while not quite coming up to the total population of Toronto, are as follows : West Toronto, 81,000 ; Centre Toronto, 41,000 ; East Toronto, 82,000. I do not understand how the hon. gentleman arrives at the figures which he has presented to the committee.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: My figures were got from a memorandum which I have before me, certified to be correct by Mr. Blue, the commissioner of the census.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Oh, oh. *

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: So far as I am concerned, I cannot go any further than that. Mr. Blue is the commissioner of the census, and he hands me as chairman of the committee this statement, and certifies it to.be correct.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The question we are considering now is as to the limits of South Toronto. The hon. member for West Toronto describes it as 200 yards wide and six miles long. The hon, member for East Toronto describes it as 200 yards wide and five miles long. There is a difference of a mile between, the two hon. gentlemen. They evidently have not studied the question very fully. If you look into the matter, you will find that they are both wrong. It is not more than four miles long, and, instead of being only 200 yards wide, it extends from Queen street southwards, crossing five or six streets down to the bay, and taking in the island-a very compact constituency, and a very reasonable and fair one. In regard to the population, how can you divide the city of Toronto into five parts and give a fairer representation than is given by this Bill ? Look at the constituencies which our hon. friends opposite would like to make. In 1892 they gave East Toronto 43,000 and Centre Toronto 26,000.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: That is not correct.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Look at East Toronto as they would propose to make it by their amendment. It is like nothing in the heavens above or in the waters beneath. It is a long, narrow strip, running along the lake shore, and running away up north and west. It is about ten miles long, and in many places you could jump across it. That is the way the hon. member fof East Toronto wants to carve out the constituency for himself. I say that the division of the city of Toronto made by the committee is not only fair according to population, but is such as to suit the convenience of the people-much more so than the division that was made in 1892 or the division proposed in the amendment by hon. gentlemen opposite. In whatever way you look at the division of Toronto, it is a fair and reasonable one, and will meet the wishes and requirements of the people of that city.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
When the Prime Minister introduced this Bill, he made very high flights of moral profession. He was going
to be so fair that no fault could be found with the redistribution by members on either side of the House. These were fine words ; but the fairness of the matter ended with the Prime Minister's speech. He delegated the practical carrying out of the arrangement to more practical men ; and we very soon discovered that one of the gentle-1 men who has had very much to do with it is very well acquainted with the game that Ah Sin was addicted to ; for there was a good deal of bluff about it. So thoroughly objectionable is the city of Toronto to the members of the government that the Minister of Trade and Commerce cannot bear to make a division of the population of Ontario without leaving out the city of Toronto, and he consoles himself by saying that if you leave out that city, there will be more Reform votes in the province of Ontario than Conservative votes ; and therefore the Reformers feel very badly that the city of Toronto is in existence. That is hardly a reasonable position for an ex-Finance Minister to take. Let us apply the same reasoning to the constituencies of North Oxford, South Oxford, Russell, West Bruce, South Middlesex and Glengarry. In these six constituencies there is a population of 143,825, and a majority of Reform votes of 4.988. The Reform votes that were polled in the whole province were 198,882. Take away from this number the number of Reform votes polled in these six ridings, 14,407, and you have 184,475 Reform votes polled in the rest of the province. If you take the total Conservative vote in the province, 203,581, and deduct from it the number of Conservative votes polled in these ridings, 9,149, you have 194,162 Conservative votes polled in the rest of the province, a majority of 9,687 over the Reform votes. That reasoning is quite on a par with the reasoning of the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce. That indicates why the committee did not do justice to the city of Toronto. They did not want to do justice to Toronto. The Prime Minister has often taunted us on this side by asking why we do not give up one member from the rural districts in order to add one to the city of Toronto. If it had been possible to have stretched the matter so far, I believe the committee would have refused to give Toronto an additional member, notwithstanding its increase of 60,000 population. They could not bluff to such an extent as to ignore that. As to the division of the city, I say it is unfair to take a long strip along the south side of Toronto and make that into a constituency. The reason given for that is that that section is practically the business and the manufacturing section of the city. The men who own the business houses and have their interests in that section of the city do not live in that section ; when they close their offices at night they go to their homes in the north, east or west of the city. If the city had been divided as the

Toronto members proposed to divide it, practically on lines running north and south, making the population as nearly equal as possible, you would have had in each constituency certain representation of the business men and of the workingmen, whereas now, with South Toronto as it is proposed, you have in that constituency practically only the business houses, banks, warehouses, and factories, while the owners of these buildings live in other parts of the town. It would have been only fair to divide the city as nearly as possible on lines running north and south so that you would have in each division of the city representation of the various Interests of Toronto. By the present Bill, you eliminate from the southern part the owners and the people who are most interested in that section. For that reason I think the division as proposed is an unfair one, and one which does not give a fair average representation of the people of the city.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. chairman of the committee (Mr. Hyman) has three or four maps to which he referred frequently to show how fair this redistribution was as compared with the previous one. Among other things he said that Yonge street was not the dividing line.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I am sure that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) does not wish to misrepresent me. I said that Yonge street was not the dividing line all the way up. Am I wrong in that?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Yes; the hon. gentleman knows very well that the only reason why there was a change at Bloor street was to equalize the population of East Toronto and West Toronto.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: That is to divide East York and West York.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Hyman) says we stopped there, not accepting Yonge as a dividing line north of Bloor and went west to Spadina. Is that right?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I think that is correct.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
The reason why in making a counter proposition we had to stop at Bloor street was that we might get an equalization of population by going from Yonge street west to Spadina and then north. The figures of population as worked out by my hon. friend from East Toronto (Mr. Kemp) and myself do not agree with the figures presented by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hyman) ; but I want to tell the hon. gentle-, man that for many years Yonge street was the dividing line between East and West Toronto. When the city had two members, Yonge street, the great artery of the city of Toronto,'was the dividing line; all east of Yonge street forming one constituency and all west of it the other. When additional representation was given to Toronto, ward boundaries were adopted. East Toronto em-Mr. OSLER.
braced St. Lawrence, St. David's, and St. Thomas' wards, West Toronto embraced St. George's St. Andrew's, St. Patrick's and St. Stephen's wards. Centre 'Toronto embraced St. James ward and St. John's ward. These were the nine wards constituting the city, and they were divided into three ridings. Under this Bill there has been added to St. Matthew's, St. Paul's, St'. Alban's and St. Mark's. And instead of making an attempt to adhere to any of the old boundaries or to any of the leading physical features of Toronto as boundary lines, these gentlemen have taken a strip from near the extreme west end of the town to the Don. I do not know how many miles, five or six, but we can easily ascertain that before the third reading. I cannot find language to characterize the principles that actuated the hon. gentlemen in making that division. They could have found fifty or sixty or seventy thousand people within two miles of where they started in the west end. But instead of that they take part of St. George's ward, part of St. James' ward, part of St. Lawrence ward, through to the Don, and stop there.-

They adopt Queen street as the northern boundary ; but Queen street is used as the northern boundary of South Toronto only as far as the Don, not to the extreme east of the city. Yet the hon. gentler man says that this is a fair thing to do.
I would like to ask what is the superficial area of Centre Toronto. Is it five miles long ? It is not half the length, and is three times the width of South Toronto. It is carved out of the centre of existing ward; boundaries, and I ask on what principle of fair play such grotesque divisions have been made ? The counter proposition was submitted as a substantial improvement on that which had been agreed upon by the hon. gentlemen ; and as my hon. friend from East Toronto (Mr. Kemp) pointed out, the two leading thoroughfares of Toronto running north and south, Yonge street and Spadina, were the boundaries, Spadina as the eastern limit of West Toronto and Yonge as the western limit of East Toronto.

speechtext:
Our only desire in Toronto and throughout the country is to get a division that is fair and right and I think the Prime Minister when he introduced this Bill thoroughly understood what would take in the province of Ontario. He knew that Ontario would appreciate a declaration that there was to be no more gerrymandering and nothing but what was fair and honest and right, that there was no desire to take advantage of their position in this House in order to create such a state of things as would place their opponents at a disadvantage. This was the statement of the Prime Minister andi the statement which went to the country. It was freely commented on and the press approved of it. No sooner, however, did we get to w'ork than we found that in this case as in some businesses there are wicked partners. The Prime Minister made a very fair statement and then he appointed the Minister of Public Works as one of the committee. Then the people of this country began to get light and to see what the object was. There was to be a fair redistribution no gerrymander-that had all disappeared. The fine hand of the Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) has been seen throughout this whole discussion, throughout all the whole dealings with this Bill. Party advantage-that has Been the object right straight through, and the country knows that what I am saying is an actual fact. He will reply that ten or twenty
years ago our friends did the very same thing. But the Prime Minister (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier), who is supposed to rule iu the councils of the government, said that we would have no more of that. I wonder that he can sit in his place and not rebuke the committee that brought in such a gerrymander to this House. Whoever heard of such a division as this of South Toronto ? But when the records of the polling divisions of the last election were brought before these gentlemen, they saw how a division of this kind would work. The figures showed to the advantage of the party of the Minister of Public Works- be is shrewd enough to see that, at any rate. And he has brought in that gerrymander, which, I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, has disgusted, not only the city of Toronto, but all fair-minded men in the province of Ontario. I have had experience of two gerrymanders-call them that, ' gerrymanders '-and I never knew one yet that did any good to the party that was responsible for it. In many cases where the old government thought they were getting an advantage by it, they found themselves defeated. And I can assure the gentlemen on the treasury benches that the same thing will result to them from one end of the Dominion to the other. We want nothing but what is fair and right; and there are no such judges of what is fair and right as are the electors of this country. The politicians may say : * Clever fellow, that Minister of Public Works ; he has arranged this thing for us.' But that cleverness does not count for much when you go to the polls. Now, the consideration of this gerrymander is approaching an end. I do not know of any concession that has been made. Perhaps they may make some. Where the gerrymander is altogether too disgraceful, as in Waterloo, they may be forced into concession- not by us. not by this House, but by their fear of public opinion in this country. We know that the province of Ontario has been gerrymandered, and we know the effect of it. What is the position of the Ontario government to-day ? Talk about the danger of one traversing this proposed riding of South Toronto falling into the bay ; why, the Ontario government are wabbling so at the present moment, we do not know which way they are going to fall ; and thenweakness is the result of just such clever, smart work as has been done here. I have no doubt that the Prime Minister intended that this should be a fair conference. Surely, in the whole Dominion of Canada some concessions might have been made. Surely, we on this side were not wrong in every instance and hon. gentlemen on the other side right in every instance. As to Toronto, this side is absolutely right. The fair way to divide the city would be to give two members to the east, two to the west and one to the centre. This proposed riding of

South Toronto is a constituency in which many of us do business, tout we live outside of it. A compact constituency was carved out called Centre Toronto, which I have the honour to represent at the present time, and in that constituency reside a good many of those who do business and have their occupation in this proposed South Toronto. But weight has been given to certain considerations. The record of the last election shows that the people who reside down near the bay gave the present government a majority in many polling divisions. I would not like to say positively that a consideration of that fact influenced the Minister of Public Works, as chairman of this committee.

It was only the day before yesterday, I think, that he rose in his place in the House after I had made what I thought was a very moderate criticism of the work of the majority of the committee and levelled the same accusation against me that he has made against my hon. friend from Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock). I asked him repeatedly to state what the abuse was and I think he came down to this point finally that lie did not think I had abused him at all. I suppose if he were asked to state in what particular my hon. friend from Centre Toronto had abused him he would be compelled to give the same answer. It is a little amusing to find the hon. Minister of Public Works always becoming pathetic whenever any criticism is made upon this Bill and regarding any criticism upon the Bill as personal abuse upon himself. I would suppose that my hon. friend after twenty-three years in the House is not a gentleman of such remarkably delicate sensibilities that he is above criticism or that any of his work is above criticism. I should hardly suppose that my hon. friend would be so sensitive on these matters as he seems to be. I certainly had no idea of abusing him and I certainly did not abuse him. I think he admitted that afterwards.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: And I think that upon reflection he will come to the conclusion that my hon. friend from Centre Toronto has not abused him.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) must have misunderstood some of the sentences I used to have the idea that I accused him in some of the remarks he made of indulging in personal abuse. I never used that language ; I do not take that position with regard to the hon. member (Mr. Brock). Every one in the House will admit that when the question was brought up by the member for Centre Toronto I gave the reasons, so far as I could, which influenced the committee in coming to this decision, and I did not attempt to say anything offensive to any one. However, the hon. member for Centre Toronto used language that was very personal, and language that was not suited to such a place as this House.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: What did I say personal 1

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gentleman (Mr. Brock) was so excited that he did not intend to use the language, which was only fitted for a very low place.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The language is taken down.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman called me the wicked partner, and he said that I had been committing political iniquities of all descriptions.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: You are exaggerating. I did not say that at all. I did not say you had been guilty of political iniquities of all kinds.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: You will see what you said in ' Hansard.'

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Yes, and you will find it is all correct.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I think the colleagues of my hon. friend (Mr. Brock) were ashamed of the extreme language he used. We might expect from the members of a great metropolitan city some reasonable discussion of the merits of the question, and not personal abuse. I do mot deny the right of the hon. gentleman to abuse me, nor do I want to recriminate on the hon. gentleman. I tried to defend myself against these attacks in a reasonable way, and I challenge him to point to any action of mine in this House, or in the committee, that would warrant him in abusing me as he has done. I know that I asume to a very great extent responsibility for the

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Bill before the House, and I 'have not tried to shirk that responsibility in any respect. I tried to meet the criticism of the opposition in a fair way, and I certainly had a' right to express my surprise that the member for Centre Toronto should use such language. Any one could see how that was accepted on both sides of the House.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: What was accepted. 1

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The speech of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Brock). The member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) had to get up In some sneering way, and instead of giving us his opinions on the Bill, he spoke of my knowledge of the great national American game. That was a great argument for a gentleman in his position to use.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman says that there has been no argument advanced from this side of the House, but he himself has not advanced a single argument to defend this Bill. He has bluffed from the beginning to the end of this discussion.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Osier) has made another of these wild statements that we hear from him so often. The Bill speaks for itself, and we take full responsibility for it. I gave my reasons for the division of the city of Toronto, and they appear in ' Hansard,' and yet the hon. gentleman gets up here and says that no reasons have been given. I am not called upon to criticise the report of the committee. It is for the hon. gentleman and his friends to show wherein it is unfair, and they have failed in that. I challenge them now to discuss the merits of the Bill, outside of their personal abuse and insinuations. Let the House be the judge as to the merits of the two propositions.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) says that the Bill speaks for itself. It is a good thing the Bill does speak for itself, because no one seems to be able to say much for it. I certainly have not heard any reason why the constituency of South Toronto should be five miles long, and in places not more than 200 yards wide. Does the Minister of Public Works regard that as a very seemly shape for a constituency ? Does he think that no better arrangement could be made than that ? The hon. gentleman may have tried to justify it, but I have not beard it, and if he has done so, perhaps he would re-state briefly the reasons that induced the committee to arrive at that conclusion. Further than that, I was led to believe, during the discussion on the county of Middlesex, that when we came to the county of York and the city of Toronto, some explanation

would lie given as to why the county of Middlesex should be regarded as one unit, irrespective of the fact that It had within it the city of London, a distinct municipal unit; and why the county of York should be treated in an entirely different way. I sought to bring my hon. friend from London (Mr. Hyman) to close quarters on that, but he told me that ample explanation would be given when we reached the county of York. We should have some explanation mow as to why one process should be applied to one county and another process applied to another county. The argument I made was thisthat you must deal with large cities like Hamilton, Ottawa, London and Toronto either on one or other of two bases. You must deal with them as distinct municipal units and fix their representation accordingly, or you must in all cases take the county and deal with it as if it did not contain a distinct important municipal unit within its boundaries. I said that if it was good logic to take the county of Middlesex, absolutely disregarding the fact that it had an important city within its boundaries, that should be good logic also for the county of York.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I submit to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden) that it is no argument at all against the fairness of a division to say that a constituency is a narrow strip. If you look over the various ridings of the Dominion you will find that there are several long narrow strips dividing two districts, along the ocean, or rivers or lakes. The chairman of the committee has pointed out that the existing division of Toronto is a long narrow strip on the front of the lake. The present division is very much narrower and very much longer, as shown on the map than the division proposed in the Bill, and yet hon. gentlemen opposite do not object to it. Representations were made to the committee that there is a community of commercial interest in what is called South Toronto, which it was desirable should be united in this constituency.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: What community of interest is it ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Commercial and manufacturing interest.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: It is commercial throughout its entire length ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I say in a general way. I am not sure that there are not some private dwellings in that district.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Of course, my hon. friend .will understand that I am not familiar with the local conditions, and I am trying to get information. I want to know the reasons which prevail in my hon.
367*
friend's mind. I understand him to say that there is a community of interest in the district and that that community of interest is a commercial interest along the whole five miles.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: That was the representation made to the committee.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman if he invited the members for the city of Toronto to make representations to him, and who were the others who advised him to take this strip along the front of the city and make a constituency out of it ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I do not know.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Who submitted the plan ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I say I do not know. It was submitted by Liberals from the city of Toronto.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: May I inquire who the gentlemen were ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I am telling my hon. friend that I do not know. If I did, I would have no objection to inform him.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Somebody presented it.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I suppose somebody presented the other plan too.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The members from Toronto presented the other plan, and they were heard before the committee, and everything they had to say there was subject to question from the Liberal members of the committee as well as the Conservative members ; but so far as I am aware, I had not the opportunity of interrogating any of the gentlemen who gave my hon. friend the information he has referred to. Of course, I do not say that that is very important, because no doubt information was conveyed to both sides by others than those who personally attended before the committee. But I merely wish to emphasize this point, that all the information placed before the committee at any formal meeting was entirely opposed to the scheme which the majority of the committee eventually adopted. I think the chairman and the hon. Minister of Public Works will bear me out in that.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The position is a very simple one. As it happens, all the members from the city of Toronto are Conservatives. The hon. gentleman will remember that no one but members appeared before the committee, except Senators in one instance.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I want to draw the attention of the committee to the fact that the hon. leader of the opposition himself objected to people who were not members being heard before the committee when I wanted to bring some from outside.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The majority of the committee had no plan before them, and there was no way of getting a plan except through friends. It is a matter of very little consequence in what way the map was submitted to us. The two plans were before the committee. As there does not unfortunately happen to be a Liberal member from the city of Toronto, the Liberal members on the committee had to consult with Liberal friends.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The cat is out of the bag at last, as far as the city of Toronto is concerned. A map was prepared by the Liberals of Toronto, who met again and again, and conned up the votes taken in the last) election. The result is that map, which is accepted by hon. gentlemen opposite as a fair division of the city, against the representations of those who have the honour to represent the city of Toronto in this House.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman says that the plan was submitted to the Liberals of Toronto, and he finds great fault because it appealed to the sense of the majority of the committee instead of the plan submitted by the Conservatives. That is about what this discussion is reduced to. It is not a discussion on the merits of the plan proposed, but is a criticism of the majority of the committee because they would not accept the extreme plan submitted by the Conservatives. As an illustration of the desire of the majority of the committee to be fair, when we were dealing with the Torontos, my hon. friend the leader of the opposition said that as these were not represented by a member of the committee, he wished to discuss the matter with his friends. In order to accommodate him, the question was postponed from time to time. His friends were called in, and in many Instances the majority of the committee accepted their views, in some cases in opposition to the wishes of our friends. That happened on more than one occasion. Well, we have before the committee these two plans for the division of the city of Toronto. Admit, if you like, that one was submitted by the friends of one political party, and the other by the friends of the other. They were there for the judgment of the committee, and hon. gentlemen opposite had the best of it, because the members for the city were present to be heard, and they are here now to be heard. If they have no better argument than unfair criticism and abuse, we must come to the conclusion that the plan submitted by the majority of the committee is the better plan of the two. If it is not, let them show on what rule or principle the proposition they make is more fair politically as between the two parties.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Is that not right ? I say if it is more fair Mr. DAVIS.
geographically, as to compactness, as to community of interest, or as to any other rule or principle that ought to govern in the consideration of this matter, let them show that. My hon. friend says what a terribly scandalous thing this is. Well, I have not seen anything about that in the Tory papers or in the independent papers of the city of Toronto, which are not very slow in howling about anything that touches them.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: They howl, do they ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Yes, and my hon. friend is apparently one of the first from the city of Toronto who would criticise this proposition if it were unfair ; but my hon. friend admits that he has no defence for the amendment.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I fancy that this community of interest, which we hear so much about for five miles along the harbour of Toronto, is marine in its character; and I should think that constituency is formed so that hon. gentlemen opposite could have Cap Sullivan to run it.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I would like my hon. friend to be as definite as he can be, in regard to this community of interest; and let me say in passing that I fully expected that before he concluded he would accuse us of abusing him, and he has fulfilled that expectation. I am sorry he cannot discuss this matter without making that accusation against us. I am trying to get along without anything of that kind ; but if he thinks we are abusing him, I am afraid we cannot dispel that feeling from his mind. Apart from that, what is this community of interest'! Is it commercial or is it not ? My hon. friend said first that it was a commercial community of interest, and then I understood him to recede a little from that.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I think the hon. member for West Toronto showed that there was a strong community of interest in the south riding.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: A political community of interest.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I think that the hon. member for West Toronto showed very clearly where the community of interest was.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I am showing it now.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I meant the hon. the junior member for Toronto (Mr. Osier).

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I made this statement, that the community of interests ceases by five o'clock. During business hours the men interested in that strip are in that part of the city, but at five o'clock the community of interest ceases and these men go to their homes in the east and west and north. There is hardly one of the men who own property and who do business in that strip, who lives in the south riding, and by this Billl yon

entirely divest a man who is interested in that constituency of political influence in it.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I must confess that it is somewhat difficult to find the exact hour at which the community of interest ceases and begins. I presume if it ceases usually at five o'clock it will cease on Saturdays at at twelve or one o'clock. As the polls close at five o'clock, I presume that the community of interest and the polls close at the same time. The hon. junior member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) has answered the argument of the hon. leader of the opposition by saying that there is a community of interest but that ceases at a certain time. There are warehouses and banks and factories and there is a community of interest.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Surely the hon. member (Mr. Hyman) is not serious in that ; a man votes where he lives.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Community of interest is what we are discussing.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: He has no vote where his interest is.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: In answer to the statement Nof the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) that South Toronto is a long narrow strip, I will not say that in many cases it will he fully a mile wide and at Yonge street it is probably three-quarters of a mile wide. At Yonge street it crosses Queen street, Richmond street, Adelaide street, King street, Colborne street, Wellington street, Front street and the Esplanade, so that it will certainly not be less than half a mile wide at that point, while in the west it will as much as a mile wide. The constituency is narrow at one point only, in the extreme west where King street and Queen street come together.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: For what district ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: 300 or 400 yards where the two streets come together. They join at an abrupt angle and are close together for only a short distance, but a glance at the map will show that at the exhibition grounds for instance it will be nearly a mile wide.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: There are no voters in the exhibition grounds.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Not on the exhibition grounds themselves, but, there are voters all about them in the adjoining streets.
At one o'clock, Committee took recess.
Committee resumed at three o'clock.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Might I inquire of the Minister of Public Works if the map which he has shows the delimitation of the proposed constituencies in Toronto ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman mean the constituencies as set forth in the Bill ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: There was no map before the committee. I had a map prepared for myself. A map was sent from Toronto on which I had marked the lines showing the constituencies. I shall be glad to show it to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Kemp).

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I suppose the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hyman) will have no objection to laying it on the Table ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Well, it is simply a map of the city of Toronto with the lines made under my direction. It is a private document, but I shall be glad to show it to the hon. gentleman.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: That is a somewhat different statement from that made by the hon. gentleman before lunch. The statement was that this map had been presented to the committee by a committee of Liberals.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I may have used the word ' map ' instead of the word ' plan,' and that may have caused the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) to misunderstand me. I may explain to my hon. friend from East Toronto (Mr. Kemp) that several propositions were sent to the committee and were discussed. The chairman, as he has said, took the map) and sketched out, from the description, the outlines of the constituencies as proposed. I would have had a map prepared, if I had thought it would have been of service.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Then, there was no map sent from Toronto to the committee?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: None that I know of.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Just a description ? The members from the city of Toronto have been perfectly frank, and have had no hesitation in being responsible for the delimination they proposed. I think it is quite reasonable for me to ask who is responsible for the propositions that were made.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I cannot understand the object of this argument, which seems to be a continuation of what was said before one o'clock. There is no question about responsibility. for. as I understand, the majority of the committee accept the responsi-, bility for the division made under the Bill.' As there is no Liberal representative from the city of Toronto, surely the hon. gentleman would not suggest that the majority in this House are to be debarred from making any recommendation that may come from the city of Toronto in regard to a matter of this kind.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: What objection can there be to stating who these gentlemen were who made recommendations ? They must he gentlemen of repute in the city.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I am sorry I have not a list to give to the hon. gentleman. I never

did have a list. I suppose I have had twenty private communications from* Toronto in regard to this matter.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Were there other communications besides this one ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: There were numbers of suggestions in regard to this matter, just as there were in reference to every constituency.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: This is the only one from which a map was made ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I do not know that a map was made from any of them. A number of voluminous statements were submitted with regard to the matter that came before the committee. And, as the majority of the committee must take the responsibility and are perfectly prepared to do so, I do not see exactly the point in the questions that are asked.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: It might possibly make the pill easier to swallow, if we knew who had put the sugar coating on it. And the country would like to know. It would have a good effect, in the interests of hon. gentlemen opposite, I am sure, if it were known what kind of people had given the advice as to this rather amusing redistribution of the city of Toronto. I happen to know the population of this South Toronto very well and may imagine where the suggestions came from and how they were justified. As hon. gentlemen opposite did not do this off their own bat, I think the country would like to know who made the suggestions ; for this is a very radical change in the city of Toronto which is a rather important constituency. The country would feel better towards the majority in this House if they knew who the gentlemen were at whose suggestion they brought in this extraordinary-I suppose I may call it without offence-gerrymander, of the city of Toronto.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
It seems to me a very reasonable thing that the questions asked by the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Kemp) should be answered. If the chairman and the majority of the committee have taken upon themselves to decline the advice given by responsible members of parliament representing Toronto, I think they ought to be prepared to say on what advice they have taken this extraordinary course of dividing Toronto in the way they have done. I have been rather desirous of getting at the facts, so far as Toronto is concerned, so that I may give an intelligent vote. I have not heard any reply why this long strip along the harbour should have been made one of the electoral divisions, entirely ignoring all the ward and municipal divisions of Toronto. I have not heard any explanation for this. I would like to know why the municipal boundaries of Toronto have been completely ignored and violated in laying out the constituencies. It seems Mr. HYMAN.
to me an outrage. There may be some reasonable explanation of it. If so, it should be given. As an outside member, one having nothing to do with the city, I think I am voicing the opinion of the country when I say that we would like to know w'hy Toronto has been thus divided up.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I can ease the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Rosamond's) mind by stating that he is mistaken when he says that the municipal boundaries have been departed from.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I understand that each constituency of Toronto, as at present divided, covers so many wards, and not divided or cut up in any way. One division may have one ward and another division two or three. Under the present arrangement they are cut up, and there is no community of interest in any constituency. This does seem to me a most remarkable course for the majority of the committee) to take.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I was satisfied the hon. gentleman (Mr. Rosamond) was mistaken as to municipal boundaries being departed from.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: But the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) has not satisfied me on that point.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: But It is the fact, as the hon. gentleman can see-

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I was referring to the ward divisions.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The ward boundaries, as I understand it, are not regarded by the hon. members from the city of Toronto as suitable for a division of the city for representation in this House. I am not very familiar with the municipal geography of Toronto, but, if I am properly informed, while there aite five members, there are six wards.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is practically correct-there are thirteen wards, but there are six divisions.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend from North Lanark (Mr. Rosamond) will see that some departure had to be made from these ward lines. The hon. members for Toronto themselves, in the plan they submitted, departed from ward lines. So, my hon. friend will see that there is no difference between us as to that. Now, I think it is time for us to lay petty politics aside and consider this matter on its merits. To do so will be much more in keeping with the dignity of this House. We have two propositions before us. I have endeavoured to point out the reasons why the majority adopted the one proposed! in this Bill. I have not heard any attempt to overcome those arguments.

Let hon. gentlemen opposite point out why the other proposition should be adopted instead of this one, and then we can choose between the two. Of course, we are entitled to our differences of opinion. The majority of the committee may be mistaken in their judgment, but, if so, let hon. gentlemen opposite show in what way we are mistaken.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I do not know what the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) refers to when he speaks of giving up ' petty politics,'-whether his allusion is to hon. gentlemen on this side of the House or the other. I am sure the question I am trying to get an answer to is a reasonable one. I ask the hon. minister again did these gentlemen who recommended this mode of redistributing the constituencies of Toronto make their views known to the minority of the committee as well as to the hon. gentleman ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Yes, I told him that I did not know the parties who made the proposition. The minority was as fully informed as the majority with regard to this proposition. I told him on several occasions that I was not aware of the gentleman who made that part of the proposition. Several were made, no one was adopted. I think when hon. gentlemen from Toronto appeared before the committee they agreed upon the proposition that is now submitted to us.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: We went up on invitation, and we entered an emphatic protest against only five members for the city of Toronto.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: True. But I kept no track, nor did any one else on the committee, of every representation that was made to us from the various constituencies as to how the division should be made. My hon. friend raises the point again as to allowing an extra member to the city of Toronto. We had to view the question in the light of the rnet that the whole province was losing six representatives, and after considering the whole matter we concluded that one extra representative to the city of Toronto would be fair enough, and that in subdividing the county of York and making practically another urban constituency, we were very liberal. There are many people in this country who trunk that we were over liberal in this respect. If the hon. gentleman can show what, in his opinion, should have been done instead of what was done, let him show it. We are willing to take the responsibility for what we have done, pleasing some and displeasing others. Under all the circumstances we think we were liberal in allowing an extra member to the city of Toronto.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
The Prime Minister, in introducing this Bill, said :
This is the Bill which I intend to move. There is a schedule attached to it. If this Bill is accepted by our friends on the other side, we intend, after it has been debated and read the second time, to refer it to a special committee composed of seven members, on which the opposition will he represented by three, to be selected by themselves. The object of the Bill will be to create the constituencies which will be allowed to elect the members of this House. In other words, we do not present to the House to-day a scheme cut and dried which has to be swallowed holus bolus by our friends and by the opposition.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Public Works made the statement that the schedules for Toronto had been prepared by his Liberal friends in Toronto-though he declines to give their names-and that was the schedule that had been accepted. Now, Toronto is Conservative by a large majority, and surely if there was any meaning in the Prime Minister's declaration which sounded so fair, then a constituency like Toronto should have had some weight in deciding the division. Lest there should be any wrong impression that this redistribution, so far as it affects Manitoba, is satisfactory, as a representative of one of those constituencies that have been most unfairly dealt with, I desire to enter my strong protest against the political nature of the division made in some of the Manitoba constituencies. To be sure I was not one of those who was credulous enough to believe that when the Prime Minister and his government decided to relegate the redistribution of the constituencies to a committee consisting of four Liberals and three Conservatives, it was an evidence that fair-play would be accorded to the Conservative party and that we would have a redistribution not marked by inequalities of population, by irregularities of outline, or by political considerations. From my knowledge of some, at any rate, of the members of that committee, I felt convinced that it was a cunningly devised plan calculated to deceive the people and to accomplish the purpose of the government under the guise of seeming fairness. My impression was further strengthened at the first meeting of the committee I had the pleasure to attend, and at which the Manitoba constituencies were dealt with. Fancy a member of a committee, called upon practically to act in the capacity of a judge and to deal out even-handed justice between the respective parties ; openly making the boast that by means of this gerrymander, for such it is, they were going to-in his own elegant language-trim the member for Marquette. Fancy having judgment passed

upon your case by so very impartial a judge, with any expectation that justice would be meted out to you. I for one did not expect justice, and I for one, have not been disappointed.

Oh, the gentleman who said that was cute enough not to have it appear on the records. Nor was it said in the committee. It was said not only to gentlemen in this House, but to gentlemen out of the House ; not to one but to half a dozen, and frcm them I received the information. Now, Mr. Chairman, the reason that this matter was referred to the committee in the first place, was not for the purpose of seeing that justice would be done, but simply because of the fact that the government could not satisfy all its followers. What would suit one government supporter would react injuriously upon his fellow-Liberal member in the neighbouring constituency, and hence, not being able to satisfy all their friends, they relegated it to a committee, calling in the opposition to assume some portion of the responsibility which they did not wish to shoulder, and still with an eye to carrying out in the main their designs. In the year 1899, a redistribution Bill was introduced into this House, and the Bill provided that where counties were large enough to send two or more members, the division within such counties should be left in the hands of the judges of the land. Great credit was taken to themselvs by the government because of their having made this first departure in the history of Canada, to remove entirely from politics the division of the different counties. If that was such an excellent principle four years ago, why should it not be equally as commendable now ? If the government could then take credit for this new departure, why have they not taken a similar course on this occasion ? Have the ministers come to the conclusion that the judiciary of the land does not stand as high in the estimation of the public as it did in 1899 ? If that is their ground, I will take no exception to that particular view. Has the Prime Minister come to the conclusion that a more fair and equitable division could be made, by, for instance, the hon. member for London (Mr. Hyman), the chairman of the committee, whose training has been in a school whose graduates have not been renowned for political righteousness ; or, by the Minister of Public Works, who has served a very long apprenticeship, and has become quite an expert as a political manipulator ; or, worse than all, by the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis), who was never known to do a fair thing by a political opponent, if there was another method that could possibly be resorted to, and who would be influenced wholly and solely by party 3C8J
and personal animus ? Did the Prime Minister thimk that fairness would be done us, if we were left to the tender mercies of these gentlemen, to whom the duty was consigned of saying whether we would have a chance for our political lives ?
