Not only did we do that, but we appeared before the committee to give all necessary explanations of that plan, to answer any questions which might be propounded to us in regard to the divisions of the province, and to give all possible informat'oj. to the best of our ability. Another plan was submitted to the committee, purporting to be the Liberal plan ; but who the father of that plan was, as in the case of the division of Toronto, we are up to the present time entirely ignorant. We endeavoured to find out its paternity, but we were refused the information. Even to this day we can only draw on our imagination as to who is the author of that plan, because none of the Liberal members of the House of Commons from Manitoba appeared before the committee to defend it, and we were forced to the conclusion that they had nothing to do with its preparation. I do not know whether they absented themselves from the committee because they were ashamed of their plan or knew that it was indefensible. If so, I appreciate their position. At any rate, we were forced to the conclusion that the Liberal members from Manitoba had nothing to do with the preparation of that plan. This impression was still further strengthened when the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis), one of the members of the committee, after hearing the evidence of the Conservative members from Manitoba, asked that the further consideration of the Manitoba constituencies be deferred until the Liberal senators from the province of Manitoba could be brought to give information. Personally I took exception to that proposal, when we had Liberal representatives of the province in the House of Commons. The chairman in reply said that when the representation of the territories was being considered, our leader had called in Senators Perley and Lougheed. But there is no parallel between the two cases, because there are no Conservative members of this

House from the territories. If there were, the hon. leader of the opposition would not have asked those senators to appear before thd committee. It seemed to us to be an extraordinary proceeding to call in members of the Senate to advise us as to the delimitation of constituencies to elect members to the House of Commons, when we had three Liberal members from Manitoba sitting in this House, not including the hon. member for Winnipeg, who generally gives his support to this government. ~As these hon. gentlemen did not appear before the committee, we came to the conclusion that they did not wish to defend their plan, and for that reason remained away. There was one peculiarity about the plan submitted on the part of the Liberals, which was in direct violation of the principle laid down by the Prime Minister. That plan provided for cutting through the boundary lines of no less than eleven municipalities. There was no defense for that proposition. It could not have been for the purpose of equalizing population, for the Conservative plan equalized the population more than the Liberal plan. The best evidence that the Conservative plan was the fairer of the two lies in the fact that many of our divisions were afterwards accepted by the Liberals, not to meet us half way, but simply because they could not defend their own scheme. One of the most glaring gerrymanders is in connection with this constituency of Dauphin and the constituency of Marquette, which I have the honour to represent. Marquette at present is composed of Marquette as it is delimitated in this Bill, along with a goodly portion of Dauphin. Owing to the increase of population and the fact that it is necessary to have three more members for Manitoba, Dauphin was made a separate constituency by adding to it a portion of Macdonald. According to the Conservative plan the population of Dauphin would be 24,209, and of Marquette 24,119. You see there is a striking equality of population, a difference of only ninety. According to the Liberal plan the population of Dauphin is 24,027 and of Marquette 20,239, a difference of two less than 4,000. In order to accomplish even that they have to divide no less than four municipalities in Dauphin, and then they go across Lake Manitoba, 25 miles, and take in a municipality called Posen-I presume, owing to the community of interest-and they add that to the constituency of Dauphin. There is no excuse for doing anything of the kind. This municipality formerly belonged to Selkirk, and even their own witness, Senator Watson, declared that there was no community of interest between Posen and Dauphin. He admitted that it could not be defended on that ground. Why, then, should Posen be put in Dauphin ? They refused to put Gilbert Plains in Marquette because they said that the community of interest between Gilbert Plains and Dauphin is more intimate than that between Gilbert Plains and the other portions of Marquette. But the local constituency of Russell, lying alongside Gilbert Plains, runs as far north as does the local constituency of Gilbert Plains, and Dauphin lies on the immediate east. They could find no community of interest between Gilbert Plains and Russell county, although they are united by a railway, but they could find community of interest or some other excuse to go across a sheet of water 25 miles wide and put Posen in Dauphin. I claim that the local municipality of Gilbert Plains had as much community of interest with the local constituency of Russell as with the local constituency of Dauphin. At one time all of that country north of the mountains was in one constituency, which I have represented up to the present time, and in that constituency at one time they had only one town, Dauphin. There was community of interest in those days, but there has been railway extension into that country, the Canadian Northern Railway runs through it and the Gilbert Plains branch extends from Dauphin town

through Gilbert Plains, through Russell, and ou to Edmontou. So that now the community of interests has entirely changed and people in the Gilbert Plains country do not go to Dauphin at all; they have their own markets in the towns of Gilbert Plains and Grand View, where they have their own judicial centres, their own agricultural societies, their own fairs, and they have no community of interest with Dauphin. In fact, as one local member said during the recent campaign, the interests of Gilbert Plains are not at all bound up with Dauphin and there is great jealousy between the two districts. Here is a railway from the town of Dauphin through Gilbert Plains and Dauphin into the local constituency of Russell, which even in this Bill is in Marquette, and still they try to make out that the community of interest of the people is with the east and not with the west, whereas the community of interests with the west will be intensified in the future because there is now a railway in course of construction, 90 miles of it already graded, and 25 miles have rails laid, through the southern part of the Riding mountains north of my own town, which is to unite with the Gilbert Plains branch in the county of Russell. The only reason given by these gentleman for taking in Gilbert Plains is that the Riding mountains, 85 miles in length, are there, and they tried to leave the impression that these mountains are a second Alps, or a second Rocky mountains, when as a matter of fact this is a gradual incline of well-timbered country, and in driving over it, as I have often done, you would not know that you were passing over a mountain. To show the House how slight the rise is, it is only necessary to give the sea levels. Near my own town of Minnedosa, in the south part of Marquette, on the southern edge of the Riding mountains, the height of land is 1,937 feet above sea level. the thing out, he will find that he has not mentioned the municipality of Roblin at all.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: All that I am suggesting is that Louise is divided into two municipalities ; both will be included in Lisgar under the name of Louise.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Roblin was not taken altogether from the municipality of Louise. Roblin was taken partly from the municipality of Louise and partly from the municipality of Turtle Mountain. It lies between the boundaries, part being included in Minto and part in Lisgar.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: In what year was it constituted.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I well get my hon. friend (Mr. McCreary) to look up the Act and we will give the hon. gentleman the information. I think my hon. friend will find that the municipality of Roblin was not taken out of Louise but that a portion was taken out of the municipality of Turtle Mountain, that it lies near the boundary between Minto and Lisgar and therefore would not be covered by section 3 of this Bill, which says:
Every town, village, township, parish or place lying within the territorial limits of any electoral district, and not specifically included in any other electoral district by the said schedule, shall be and be taken to be part of the electoral district in which it is so locally situate.
It would not apply to the municipality of Roblin inasmuch as part of it is in one constituency and part in another. Therefore, I think you will find that it will have to be looked at again. I have proved conclusively to the committee that the hon. member for Marquette has divided the municipality of Howard. 'By reference to the Act he "will find that my statement is correct. I also want to inform the hon. gentleman that notwithstanding the statement he made a while ago he Is incorrect about Roblin and that he will find that he proposes to divide it. If he looks into it he will find that what I say is correct.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: No, I have just looked into it again.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Well, I think he should look into it again. I want to allude to the fact that in making the local divisions of the constituencies in Manitoba, the Roblin government now in power in Manitoba, adopted the same principle exactly that the committee have adopted in dealing with this question. Not only have the Roblin government adopted that principle but the previous government adopted it also. I want to tell the hon. member for Marquette and the hon. leader of the opposition that this principle has always been adopted and that it always will be adopted, I think, in the north-western portion of this country because there

is a permanency about the township and range system that does not exist with the municipal boundary lines which are changing from time to time. By reference to the Act for the division of the province of Manitoba into electoral divisions assented to on the 18th of March, 1903, it will be seen that :
The expressions ' parish,' ' settlement,' * lot,'
* section,' ' township ' and ' range,' and the numbers thereof referred to, mean a parish, settlement, lot, section, township and range, respectively, in Manitoba, according to the systems of survey authorized hy the * Dominion Lands Act ' of the parliament of Canada and used by the government of Canada, and the numbers thereof according to such systems.
Go through the Act and you will find that municipalities are not mentioned at all. They have adopted the same system that we have adopted in making this redistribution in Manitoba because there is a permanency about the township and range system that there is not about the municipalities. I will give, for instance, the description which the Manitoba Act gives of Springfield :
The electoral division of Springfield shall comprise townships numbered eleven and twelve, whole or fractional, sections numbered from one to five, from eight to twelve, from thirteen to fifteen, from twenty-two to twenty-seven and from thirty-four to thirty-six, inclusive of all such numbers, in townships numbered ten all in range numbered four east, except the north-west quarter of section number seven, &c.
Ill describing every section in Manitoba, the local government have stuck to the township and range system, and the previous; government did the same thing. The committee merely followed out the rule which has been laid down. We who live in the west know the advantage of adopting that rule and if the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche) was not affected so seriously as he thinks he is, he would admit that it is a proper system to adopt in that country. I do not think there is anything in the criticism that the hon. gentleman offers as far ns dividing municipalities is concerned. When the right hon. leader of the governr ment laid down the rule which should guide the committee and which was that county boundaries should be adhered to, I pointed out that there were no county boundaries in Manitoba, but that there were a lot of municipalities that were changing from year to year. The majority of the committee took that into consideration and they adopted the system which has been pursued by both Liberal and Conservative governments in the province of Manitoba and which is the only system that could be adopted in making a redistribution in the west. That was the principal grievance, I think, that the hon. member for Marquette had, although he dealt to some extent with the division of the riding of Dauphin. I have a map here showing the proposition Mr. DAVIS.
that was made by hon. gentlemen opposite. These hon. gentlemen in the fulness of their hearts, probably thinking that they still had power to carry out their plans, in place of coming before the committee with a fair proposition, brought forward a map-I do not blame the hon. leader of the opposition for it, because he had to consult his political friends from the west-and tried to fix up a gerrymander to suit themselves so that they could get back into this House.
I will leave it to any unbiased man in this House to look at these two propositions and tell me which is the fairer plan on the face of it. In the plan which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Roche) proposes he has gone away out to the extreme corner of the province of Manitoba, away down near Saskatchewan near the Pas, and he has run the line of the constituency right close to Portage la Prairie. The hon. gentleman talks about a community of interests. Will he tell me what community of interests there is between the people who fish in the northern part of that country and the people who grow grain in the vicinity of Portage la Prairie ? Does he know the length of the constituency which he proposes ? It is over 200 miles long.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: And you have gone still further to the east of the lake twenty-five miles. You have gone fishing.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: According to the plan laid on the Table of the House the municipality of Posen has been taken from the east side of Lake Manitoba and put into Dauphin. But these gentlemen opposite who talk about community of interests, propose to cut up the Icelandic settlements and to put some o.f the Icelanders in with the French in Macdonald, some into Selkirk and some into Dauphin. If it is wrong to put a whole municipality on the south side of the lake into Dauphin, it must be equally wrong to put part (if it into Selkirk, part of it into Macdonald and part of it into Dauphin. Our proposition is much fairer to the people themselves, and makes a much more compact constituency.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: What municipality are you referring to '!

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I speak of the residents of Posen, but I think it is not a municipality.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: It is an unorganized district. Now, as to the constituency of Marquette.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
It is a fact that the provincial government have always observed that range of mountains as a dividing line, and they did that because there was a community of interest there which should not be overlooked. In order to show the spirit of fairness in which the member for Marquette approached this question, I read from his remarks before the committee :

A deputation from Dauphin has been down here and I heard that a gentleman who was aspiring to represent the oonstitueney has been here in consultation endeavouring to get the constituency carved out so that he can carry it. If you will allow me to go into the political aspect of the two plans regarding Marquette, I may say there is considerable difference. I may also say that when I saw the map I was not at all surprised because I heard before that it was a plan that was going to defeat me at the next election, and I am nor sure but that it will have that effect. There is 350 of a nominal majority on the south side of the mountain and I get my minority on the other side.
In other words, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Roche) wanted this committee to sit down and carve out a constituency to suit him. He thought that ail we were there for was to make political constituencies for gentlemen who appeared before us, and he was surprised that the committee did not take that into consideration at all. He complained that a certain gentleman from Dauphin came here to get the constituency carved out so that he might carry it in the Liberal interest, but in the next breath the member for Marquette said that we were taking away from his constituency several municipalities that gave him large Conservative majorities and throwing them into Dauphin. That is logic for you. Surely if we take away three or four municipalities from Marquette and throw them across the mountain into Dauphin we are not strengthening this gentleman who came down here to have a Liberal constituency arranged for him. We could not carry out ottr proposition without injuring that gentleman. I allude to that to show how much the argument of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Roche) is worth.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: To show how little you know about it.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman says that in the case of Marquette community of interest is no.t taken into consideration. If he looks at the plan he will find that there is a land district on the north side of the mountain, and every one knows that the business of the settlers is done where the land office is, so that the community of interest is preserved under our proposition. Under the Conservative plan they throw a portion of the land district of Dauphin into Marquette and destroy the community of interest. The fact that the member for Marquette says be could drive over the mountain does not prove that it is not a natural barrier. He must know that the timber reserves on the top of the mountain have been sold by the Dominion government, and that here are only three roads across the mountain, but in order to carve out a constituency for him he wants us to go over the mountain and place the people of Gilbert Plains in his constituency. Surely it
was not the business of the committee to gerrymander in the interests of the hon. member for Marquette. And now as to population. The unit of population in Manitoba is 23.665, omitting the city of Winnipeg, and the hon. gentleman (Mr. Roche) complains that under our plan the population of the riding is only 20,467, whereas by his proposition it would be 24,615.
My hon. friend knows his own constituency. Does he mean to tell me that people are not going in there ? A branch line, which the government of Manitoba has subsidized, is being built through a portion of that constituency, and if it is not going to have the effect of bringing a large number of people in there, what is it being built for ? At the other end of his constituency is the Great North-west Central branch of the Canadian Pacific Railway, which will also have the effect of increasing the population. So that it will not be very long before his constituency will have more people than the unit." If hon. gentlemen opposite are so very anxious to stick to the unit, I would like to ask them what about Selkirk ? The hon. gentleman has not told us that all that yeanling anxiety in regard to the unit did not seem to strike them when they came to deal with Selkirk. This riding although there are a lot of Indians in it, they reduced to 19,000 odd. They did not stick to the unit there, because it did not suit their political ideas to do so. Our plan gave Selkirk 24,029, a few hundreds over the unit, whereas their plan gave it 19,339. If it is fair, in carving out a constituency, to have regard to community of interest and to the prospects of new settlement coming in, and if it is fair to give Selkirk 19,339, it surely ought to be equally fair for the hon. gentleman to accept a constituency with a population of 20,553. Now, I will read the populations proposed under both plans, to show that there is an agreement. For Brandon the population of both parties is the same, 25,047, a little over the unit. For Dauphin our plan gives 22,387, while their plan gives 24,259.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: How does the hon. gentleman compute the populations where the municipalities are divided ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: This population was taken from the census returns and worked out, and I think the hon. member will find it much more correct than his own.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I worked it out, and made it different from the hon. gentleman's statement.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I will show where the hon. gentleman is wrong in some cases. The map which was prepared and handed into the committee by the committee members, with the accompanying amendment of the proposed constituencies in Manitoba, differs

from the plan outlined in tlieir schedule ; so that their schedule as presented to the House did not correspond with their plan. The schedule places the whole of Louise as it existed before the formation of Roblin municipality into Lisgar constituency, whereas the map placed Louise as it now exists in Lisgar, the part which was taken away to [DOT] form part of Roblin going to the constituency of Minto. The schedule places township 28 in ranges 21, 22, 23, 24 and 25, in Dauphin, whereas the map places them in Marquette. The schedule places all of the unorganized districts of Schultz and Wimii-pegosis in Selkirk, whereas the map places only such part or parts as lie east of range 7 west. So that the hon. gentleman will see that he is not infallible, but has made a lot of mistakes. Take the constituency of Dauphin. The figures given in the schedule are 24,209, whereas the right figures are 24,259. The difference is not very great, but it is a difference of 50. Take the constituency of Marquette. The figures placed before the House by the hon. gentleman opposite showed the population of his own constituency to be 24,128, whereas as a matter of fact it had a population of 24,615, a difference of 487. Take Selkirk, they have put it down at 19,886, whereas as a matter of fact it has only 19,339. Taking the whole proposition into consideration, we will fiud that the plan submitted by the Liberal members on the committee is the fairer one of the two. The very fact that we have agreed in the case of Brandon and several other cases goes to show that a spirit of fairness was manifested by the committee ; and what thanks do we get for that ? The hon. member for Marquette says that we intended to take the constituency of Argyle away from Souris, the county to which it belonged, and put it into Portage la Prairie ; and be goes on to picture the range of mountains, the streams and the lakes in that municipality. I want to tell him that the streams and mountains and lakes are all there yet, and if he looks at" the map he will see them. All these things show the spirit of fairness with which the committee were prepared to deal with these gentlemen. When it was shown that some injustice was likely to be done to my hon. friend from Macdonald, they at once rectified it and gave him what he wanted. Take the ease of Proveneher. The hon. member for Marquette stated that we were tearing that constituency to pieces, and placing the home of my hon. friend who represents Proveneher in another constituency. Well, I do not think it was ever supposed that we were to carve the constituencies to suit any particular person. We are here to carve them in such a way as to make ns fair a division as we possibly can in the interests of the people, and in Manitoba 1 think we have pretty nearly done that. Take the case of Macdonald, or Dufferin, as hon. gentlemen call-Mr. DAVIS..
ed it in their plan. They ran it from near Brandon away north on the line of the Canadian Northern Railway, and then ran it like a belt to Lake Manitoba on the other side. No one ever saw such a gerrymander. We have made it a compact constituency, with a community of interests among the people, and I think any person who examines it will acknowledge that it is a fair division. Take the constituency of Selkirk.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I beg to draw the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that that is not a correct map.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman produce the correct map ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: It is in the hands of the committee.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman will find that this is the same.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: We submitted a second map to the committee, and the members of the committee know perfectly well that that is not the revised plan:

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman want to see the first map ? If he does, I will send for it. The hon. gentleman was not satisfied with his gerrymander the first time, and he had to come down with a second one.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I would ask the chairman of the committee (Mr. Hyman) for the map which the hon. gentleman has in his possession. The hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) has the map on which the schedule was based and I would ask if he did not request us to leave our revised map in his possession. He has that map and I asked the other day to have it laid on the Table.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: That is the map I laid on the Table the other day.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: It is not.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: This is exactly the map. The hon. gentleman had two maps ; they have one slipped up their sleeves.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: So had the Liberals, they changed their map too.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I hold in my hand the first map and 1 do not think it is any improvement on the second map. I would like to point out tb the committee the shape of the constituency of Dauphin as preposed by hon. gentlemen, which is indicated by the lines to which I am pointing. I would like to know where the community of interests is between the municipalities associated in that map. One object in the divisions as proposed by them is to divide the Icelandic vote which they know is principally Liberal. They desire to cut it in two and to put one-half of it in with the French settlers. I would draw attention to the irregularity of other constituencies and would ask hon.

members if the special committee should be blamed because they did not accept ail the suggestions contained in this map. We accepted nearly two-thirds of their suggestions ; we accepted Brandon, Lisgar and Provencher. Then let us look at Marquette, The hon. gentleman (Mr. Roche, Marquette) wishes to take in municipalities north of this chain of mountains, for it is a chain of mountains and is covered with timber. The statement which I read from the evidence of the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche) shows why he desired to have this done. He made the statement that on the other side of the mountain he was over 200 short and he was afraid he might be defeated under this redistribution. For that reason he asked the committee to go over the mountain and take in a couple of the municipalities so that he could be returned in future.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman. as usual is drawing on his imagination. He stopped short in reading my evidence and did not read the part in which I claimed that while I did not want to have any favour done me in the division of this riding I did not want any injustice either and an injustice is being done now.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I would like to know where the injustice comes iu. AVe have followed the boundaries of their friends in making the distribution of Manitoba. AA'e have adopted the divisions as they are constituted by them for land title purposes and for municipal purposes and yet the hon. gentleman, who is upholding municipal boundaries, now wants to go across the mountains and take in two other municipalities.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: In what constituency has that district north of the mountains been in during the last six years.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
The whole Dauphin country and away to the North Pole was in the hon. gentleman's constituency, and the hon. gentleman is sitting in this House through the good will of the people in the north of the constituency. Now he is anxious to have them in his constituency still in order that he may be again returned to this House. I have no objection to that, I would like to see him back, but I do not think he should ask the committee to gerrymander a constituency to suit him.	*

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Before you left the Chair at six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I had not time to go over the list that was handed to me, but I have gone over it since, and I find that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) is perfectly right, so far as Brandon is concerned. It was put at the bottom and has been overlooked by the parties who made up the list. However, as to the other constituency that I have mentioned, that is Roblin, I wish to show the hon. leader of the opposition and the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche) that I was perfectly right about the matter. I have here the statute of Manitoba for 1902. I read :
The rural municipality of Roblin shall comprise townships 1 and 2 in ranges 13, 14 and 15, west of the principal meridian.
Now, I would point out that, according to their last plan, townships 1 and 2, in range 15, west of the principal meridian is in what they call Minto, while townships 1 and 2, in ranges 12,13 and 14 are in Lisgar. So, there is actually a division of the municipality of Roblin. Then, if the hon. gentleman will go back to the rural municipality of Louise, he will find that is all in Lisgar. On that point, I am perfectly correct. AVliile I was in error with reference to Brenda, I wish to draw the attention of the leader of the opposition to one fact on the other side. The riding of Macdonald, as he has laid it out in his plan, is intended to include Portage la Prairie, Portage la Prairie town. North and South Norfolk, North and South Cypress and Carberry. But there is in the riding of Macdonald a municipality called Victoria, which apparently, the hon. gentleman did not know anything about. It is possible that the population of Victoria may have been included with that of some of the other municipalities in their estimates. But that does not affect my argument, for the fact remains that these municipalities are changing so much that the leader of the opposition in getting up his schedule did not know what municipalities there were in this constituency of Macdonald.
Now, I do not think it is fair for hon. gentlemen on the other side to accuse the committee of gerrymandering the province of Manitoba. The facts show that there was no such design on the part of the committee. Let me draw the attention of the leader of the opposition and the hon. member for Provencher (Air. LaRivierol that, had it been the intention of the committee to gerrymander Alanitoba, it would have been very easy for us to arrange to make two more seats safe for the Liberals. I think the hon. member for Provencher will bear me out that it would have been easy for us to cut out Letellier and another little corner called St. .Toe, and throw them into Minto or Souris. I think the hon. gentleman will agree that if this were done, his chances of election would be very slim indeed.
Air. LaRIATERE. My hon. friend (Mr. Davis) knows that what he did not try in the south he tried in the north. It is true, he withdrew it when I pointed out that it was unfair.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
In the north it would only he necessary to throw a part into Macdonald to make Macdonald safe for the Liberals and cripple him (Mr. LaRivifere). In this way we could have made both Provencher and Macdonald safe for the Liberals. This is what the government might have done had they desired to serve the Conservatives as they served us years ago. I think the government deserve no small credit for what they have done In Provencher. There is a constituency that, for years, has returned a Conservative to this House. It is a constituency in which the French speaking people have a large majority. Those people have a representative here, sitting for a constituency where he is absolutely safe. And, though it is against their political advantage, yet, out of consideration of the community of interest, they leave that constituency where it is. Surely they deserve some credit for that. And they deserve some credit for arranging some of the other seats to suit hon. gentlemen opposite. The whole proposition in Manitoba has been a case of give and take, and hon. gentlemen opposite, as I have said, got the best end of the stick. Surely they do not expect it all. Surely they do not expect tins committee, with its majority of one in favour of the government, of which these hon. gentlemen have said so much, to sit down and make seats for them. The committee did the best they could under the circumstances ; and I think it is most unfair to accuse the committee of partisan* ship or to point to individual members as partisans who tried to knife every Conservative who has a seat in this House. The facts do not bear out any such statement. We submitted our plan, and hon. gentlemen opposite submitted theirs. And it is for hon. gentlemen opposite to show, taking population, community of interest and every other element into consideration, but leaving politics aside, why their plan is better than ours. I still believe that ours is the better plan, but if these hon. gentlemen do not think so, let them give their reasons for their opinions. That will be better than merely calling the members of the committee partisans and unfair judges. Of course, these hon. gentlemen must know that no redistribution committee *can satisfy every one. If a little piece is taken from or added to a member's constituency, he is very apt to say that he is being injured politically, and that the Act is a gerrymander. Some members from Manitoba may feel sore, but, taking the province as a whole, I claim that the redistribution given in the final plan of the committee is far better than that in the plan submitted by hon. gentlemen opposite. If they do not think so, it is for them to show wherein theirs is better than ours.
Now, with reference to the plans, I have before me a plan which is a copy of the last plan submitted by the minority on the com-
Mr. LaRIVIERE.
mittee. The minority, I understand, submitted two plans, if they submitted three, I do not know anything about the third. But I have the two plans here, and I will hand them over to the member for Marquette so that he can see wherein it differs to any extent from the one which he claims was finally presented by them to the committee. I think the chairman of the committee has pointed out that a line running out from Lake Manitoba through Dauphin has thrown a little more territory into Dauphin. If that is the case, it does not appear to meet the views of the hon. member for Marquette. But when he was before the committee, as I find by page G3 and G4, he had this to say with reference to Selkirk :
The argument in favour of our plan fcr Selkirk as compared with that of our Liberal friends, is that they want to make the constituency of Dauphin too large, and it is necessary to divide the territory.
That is the reason he lays down why their plan for Selkirk was better than ours. Now, I want to say that by their division they did make Selkirk larger than it was proposed by the Liberals to make Dauphin. They wanted to divide the territory equally, but in their distribution they made Selkirk a great deal bigger than we proposed to make Dauphin. However, here is the plan, and I will hand it over to the member for Marquette, and if there is any difference between the two plans he will be kind enough to show it. Before taking my seat I would like the leader of the opposition to figure out that municipality of Howard. As I have pointed out, that lies in the constituency of Selkirk, and also in that of Provencher ; also the municipality of Rob-lin lies partly in Dufferin and partly in Lis-gar. If they are sticking to municipal boundaries, how does it come that these municipalities are divided up ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Lest there might be some hon. gentlemen opposite who are credulous enough to take stock in all these exaggerated statements of the member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis), which he is rather prone to, I desire to contradict some of them very briefly, because I realize in advance that we are fighting an uphill battle, with no prospect whatever of having our views adopted ; in fact, I realized that before I went into the committee at all. Now, the member for Saskatchewan has stated that we were endeavouring to gerrymander the pi'ovinee of Manitoba to suit ourselves. Well, these four hon. gentlemen composing the Liberal majority on the committee must be very innocent indeed if they were going to allow the three Conservative members in Manitoba to gerrymander that province in our interest, when, they had a majority on the committee. When we come to compare our plans in the first place, in order to make our task lighter, we ad-

mitted to the chairman that we knew very little about other constituencies outside of our own. We asked him to submit to us the Liberal plan, and if in our judgment we thought that plan was satisfactory and according to the principles laid down by the Prime Minister, we would adopt it; if not, we would improve it to the best of our ability. We got that plan and we were guided by it. Where we made a deviation from the Liberal plan it was in accordance with the principle laid down by the Prime Minister, that is, where we found a municipality divided, we included the whole of that municipality, and that is the principal difference between the two plans. Now he states that there is no argument so far as Manitoba is concerned, in the original municipal boundaries, because they are continually changing. In any new country, we know that the boundaries of constituencies and municipalities will be changing, because of the influex of population making that necessary. But the municipalities that have been changed largely by the provincial Act of recent years, have been municipalities where the population, was dense enough to require a division into two. Take for instance what was done last session. There were two municipalities in my riding which were populous enough to divide into three, but that did not interfere with the boundaries of the original municipalities. When the description in the local Act and in this Bill is given by township and range, the adoption of municipal boundaries does not prevent the description being given by township and range. You may do that and still not violate municipal boundaries. The member for Saskatchewan says there is nothing at all in this description of municipal boundaries, because there are no municipalities, practically, in Manitoba. I would ask the hon. gentleman if he does not think that when a municipality is organized and has its own council selected in the same way as the county councils are selected in Ontario, if he does not think that when they have their municipal organization, some importance should be attached to it, and that a portion of it should not be taken away and attached to another municipality where they have no community of interests. That is what they have done in connection with the division of municipalities in the province of Manitoba. There each municipality is divided into wards, and elects its municipal councils. It has an organization the same as that of the county council in the province of Ontario. The hon. gentleman has referred to the municipality of Roblin as being a portion in the electoral riding of Souris and another portion in Lisgar. He is wrong. If he looks at the wording of the Revised Statutes he will find that the division line, between the constituency of Lisgar and the constituency of Souris is the same as in ours. The municipality of Louise is entirely in the
electoral riding of Lisgar, and the municipality of Roblin is entirely in the municipality of Souris.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: If you can find range 15 in that according to your plan, I will acknowledge that I am mistaken. Fifteen is in Minto.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Ranges 13, 14 and 15 are all in the electoral riding of Souris, and the municipality of Roblin extends west of range 13. The hon. gentleman says that the local electoral ridings violate municipalities. As I say, they are described in the Act by township and range, and while the local Act does not maintain municipal boundaries in every respect, in Mr. Roblin's speech in introducing the Redistribution Bill of last session, as I gave evidence before the committee, he distinctly said that while on all occasions they would not observe municipal bftundaries, nevertheless that would be the chief object in his Redistribution Bill, that they would violate them to the least possible extent.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: How many municipalities did the recent division of Manitoba split up ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I am not acquainted with that.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Twenty-two.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: No, a very small number in proportion to the whole. The hon. gentleman states that Posen is not a municipality.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Posen was disorganized seven or eight years ago, and it has not been reorganized.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The Revised Statutes of Manitoba, 1902, gives a list of all the municipalities right up to this year, and in that list I find it stated that the rural municipality of Posen shall comprise townships numbered so and so, the same as every other municipality. If you look at the map you will see Posen.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: There has not been a reeve and council or officials elected for the municipality of Posen for the last seven or eight years.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
We are not supposed to know that. We know by the map and by the statutes that Posen occupies the same position as if it was a municipality. And were we dividing that territory the hon. gentleman would be the first to get up and object to it, stating that we would be putting one portion of the people in one division and another portion of the people in another division. The hon. member for Saskatchewan has stated that the Liberal candidate, or presumptive Liberal candidate, who is going to contest Dauphin cannot be assisted in any way and that I am entirely inconsistent in claiming that by

Gilbert Plains being put into Marquette it would give the Conservatives a majority of 200 in that constituency, but if it is retained in Dauphin how can it assist the Liberal candidate there ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I did not say Anything of the kind. I said that this argument was a weak one, and that if this municipality were thrown into Dauphin, I did not understand how it was going to help the Liberal candidate in Dauphin by 200 or 300 votes.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
That is a point I am going to explain. The hon gentleman is not acquainted with the local conditions, because, if he were, he would not have spoken in that way. In the present Dominion electoral riding of Marquette I could not be elected were it not for the liberality of the Liberals who reside there. The Conservatives are so much in the minority that I could not get alonfe without the vote that I get from the Liberals. The district of Dauphin has been represented for two terms in the local legislature by a relative of the hon. Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Sifton), Mr. Burrows, and he was able to carry that constituency against the Conservatives. He carried it by grace of the Conservative majority, although no other man could. Mr. Burrows is a strong man in that constituency. He has large vested interests there. He is a large mill-owner, a large employer of labour ; and, therefore, he would not be injured by retaining Gilbert Plains in Dauphin, whereas hon. gentlemen know perfectly well that it would assist in electing a Conservative if that municipality were placed in Marquette. The hon. gentleman undertool; to refer to a portion of the evidence that I gave before the committee, and he stated that I wished the constituency to be gerrymandered so as to assist in 'being elected by putting these 200 votes in Gilbert Plains into the constituency of Marquette. I asked him to read on a little farther and he would show the Committee that I was not asking any favour from the Redistribution Committee, because I do not ask that this shall he done in favour of myself. All I ask for is fair-play, and I do not expect even to get that. When I appeared before the committee I made the following remark :
If you allow me to go into the political difference I may say it is considerable, and I may also say that when I saw the map I was not at all surprised, because I heard before that it was the plan that was going to defeat me at the next election.
I was not surprised when I saw this plan that the Liberals produced before tlie committee, because I had been told by my Liberal opponents during tliis past year, and before this parliament assembled, that this was the division which was going to be made, and that it was going to be made for the purpose of defeating me at the next election. The chairman asked me :

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Will it have that effect ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I am not sure but it will. There is 350 of a normal majority on this side of the mountain and I get my majority on the other side.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I could not understand before why there was so much importance attached to this. I had no idea there wTas anything of that kind.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I am not asking any favour from the committee because of political complexion, but I am asking that no injustice should be done me on account of political complexion.
That shows that I was not asking for Gilbert Plains to be put in to assist me, but I was asking that I should not be militated against, simply because of Gilbert Plains being on the Conservative side of politics. The hon. gentleman states that the diversity in population between Marquette and Dauphin will easily be made up, because people are going into Marquette. Marquette is ail old settled portion of the country. It is not filling up as rapidly as Dauphin is. Dauphin is a comparatively new constituency. It has only been erected into three electoral ridings during the last session of the local legislature. The Canadian Northern Railway has been In course of construction up through that northern country, and people have been flocking in there much more rapidly than they have into Marquette, so that the diversity of population which exists now will be intensified in the course of the next ten years. Hon. gentlemen must remember that we are legislating for the next ten years, and not for the present alone. Dauphin will have several thousand more people than Marquette if this plan goes through, and in ten years time, owing to this influx of population, the difference will be very much greater than It is at the present time. The hon. gentleman has also stated that the Kirkella branch runs through the western part of the constituency, and that people will be flocking into old Marquette. The Kirkella branch does not run through my constituency at all. It runs through the North-west Territories, and will have no effect on my constituency. Then the hon. gentleman took exception to our figures as to population, and when I asked him where he got the population that is placed in the schedule of hon. gpi'Hnm.en opposite, the only reply he made was that I had the schedule and that I could figure it out. He did not even figure it out himself, and yet he took exception to the schedule that we produced. I find that the population, as provided for in our schedule, docs not exactly coincide with that of the schedule prepared by the hon. gentleman's friends, although the difference is very slight in some instances. As far as the plan for Dauphin is concerned, the hon. gentleman, before six o'clock, undertook to make considerable game of our constituency of Dauphin. He went on to say that it zig-zagged all over

and he wanted to know what all these steps meant. This is the constituency according to the map that is iiroduced. It starts away up to the north and ends away down near Portage la Prairie. The reason that it extends so far north is that there is no population up there. The district between the two lakes, according to the last division of the constituency of Dauphin, was placed in Selkirk, and a line was simply run through, because there is unorganized territory in which no people are living.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Why was it necessary, if there is nobody living in that district, to make all those steps ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: When exception was taken to these vsteps, it was thought by hon. gentlemen opposite that there was some political significance in that arrangement, and to show how little there was in the argument, <we said : We will lay aside that plan and run this line in another direction. Our plan is a good one for the division of the constituency of Dauphin as compared with that of hon. gentlemen opposite. When you are finding fault with the division of Dauphin, you must remember that the Liberal division goes six townships farther east and makes Dauphin thirty-six miles greater in breadth than the Conservative plan. There was no political significance in this plan, which was discarded because exception was taken to it. Senator Watson declared that north of Posen there were not more than 300 souls between these two lakes. As far as the two plans are concerned, and as far as Selkirk is concerned, Selkirk is made more compact for the hon. gentleman, who represents that constituency by the Conservative plan, and he has 200 or 300 mort-iof a majority. I would just as soon that he got that advantage as any other- Liberal candidate. The division that we propose would have divided Selkirk on the east and Dauphin on the west almost in the centre territorially. The hon. gentleman states that we go away down south to the wheat fields of Portage la Prairie. We have made a departure from the Liberal map, but in doing that we only followed out the principle laid down by the Prime Minister, that municipal boundaries must be adhered to, and we innocently thought that principle would be carried out. And as to community of interest : if there is no community of interest in this case with Dauphin, how could you have community of interest with the people east of the lake twenty-five miles away ? The Liberal plan provides that Posen, which is located west of the lake, shall be taken into this constituency, where the people never see each other from one end of the year to the other. They have no railway communication ; they cross on dog sleds in the winter, when the lake is frozen, and by row boats in the summer.

speechtext:
The member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis), who was a member of the committee whose report we are now considering, spoke for upwards of an hour on the general question of the redistribution in Manitoba, as contained in this Bill. I listened to all he said, and I discovered that his idea of the redistribution in Manitoba consists only of nine seats. I understand that this is practically his redistribution, and I wondered on what principle he had conducted it. In introducing this report to the House, the chairman of the committee submitted a table in which it was stated, that the population of Manitoba was 255,211 giving a unit of 25,252 for the ten seats and I may inform the hon. gentleman (Mr. Davis) that there are going to be ten seats in Manitoba, and not nine. Now, according to another table submitted by the chairman of the committee, we find that out of the ten Manitoba seats, eight are allotted to constituencies that are below the unit. We find that one constituency, that of Portage, has a population of 27,732 or 2,000 beyond the unit, and the tenth seat, that of Winnipeg, has 17,000 above the unit. On the face of it, this redistribution is suspicious,
I must draw the conclusion that there must have been some plan or rule followed in al-



lotting these seats, and I am curious to know from the hon. gentleman (Mr. Davis) what kind of a rule gave this result. The member for Saskatchewan in referring to the constituency of West Selkirk, which has a population of 20,000 mentioned that there were quite a large number of Indians in that riding. Now as a matter of fact in the city of Winnipeg with its population of
42,000,	there are practically no Indians* at all. In the province of Manitoba there are six thousand Indians, and all of those are in the rural districts. As a matter of fact there are only eight Indians counted in the population of the city of Winnipeg, and the balance of the six thousand are outside of Winnipeg, so that for the purpose of parliamentary representation we may reduce the population of Manitoba outside of Winnipeg by the 6,000 Indians, and that makes the unit of representation in Winnipeg all the larger. Is it not a fair question to ask the member for Saskatchewan, what rule was laid down which gave such an allottment of ten seats to the province of Manitoba ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: My bon. friend (Mr. Puttee) has heard the rule discussed for the la#two or three days. I would like to see the city of Winnipeg getting two members, but I have always held, and I still bold, that where we have a compact city covering only two or three miles square, with morning papers,, street cars, messenger service, telephones and telegraphs, one member can better represent 45,000 people, than a member can represent 20,000 in a rural district where there are none of these conveniences, and where the population is scattered all over the constituency. You have the member in a city in touch with his people. There is not one constituent of the hon. member (Mr. Puttee) who cannot see him within fifteen minutes of his office, but in the rural district it is different.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: It was not my purpose to discuss the representation of the city of Winnipeg under this amendment ; but I wish to say that if the hon. member who has just sat down had wished to give that city two members, he could have done so. He says it is not necessary, because the cities are represented by other members who live in them besides their own representatives. Well, Sir, if that argument was applicable to Winnipeg in the past, it does not look to me as if it would be in the future ; because if future sessions are going to last as long as this one has lasted, members who represent western constituencies are going to live in the city of Ottawa, and it will be totally impossible, as it has been for the last six months, for a constituent of mine to come down to my office. Talking on this same subject last evening, the chairman of the committee, the hon. member for London (Mr. Hyman), also stated that it had to be taken into

consideration that a large number of members representing rural constituencies lived in cities, and that these cities had the benefit of their advocacy ; and he referred to the number living in Montreal and Toronto. But that remark does not apply to the city of Winnipeg, where there is only one western man living besides myself, that is, the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) ; and he is the member for Selkirk and jnat for Winnipeg. We have both been living in Ottawa more than in Winnipeg since we have been elected. So that that argument, although it may have some weight with reference to the eastern cities, has no application whatever to Winnipeg. This is what the hon. member for London said :
In Montreal there are ten senators and ten members living in that city. Toronto has twelve members and senators combined who are residents, and Montreal has twenty senators and members combined, a total ,of thirty-two for the two cities. Taking the average representation of Canada, I find there is one member for each 25,000 inhabitants, and taking the number of members living in Montreal and Toronto, I find there is one member for each 26,432. If that is a fair argument, the unit in Montreal and Toronto is only 1,432 less than in the rural constituencies. And when we combine members and senators, we find that on the average there is a representative in either House for a population of 18,331, while in the cities of Montreal and Toronto there is a member or a senator for each 14,867.

I would ask the hon. gentleman to inform me of the rule by which this arrangement was worked out. What convinces me of that is that the member of the committee who had this matter specially in charge, spoke for an hour and referred all the time to the other constituencies.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Item 10 reads :
The electoral district of the city of Winnipeg, which shall continue to be constituted as at present.
I would submit to you that any reasonable man would be struck at once with the idea that that is a very remarkable statement, that the city of Winnipeg, the most rapidly growing city in the country, a city which is destined to be a large city, the Chicago of the west, shall for ten years more be constituted as at present. That means that it is to have a single representative in this parliament. I shall take the census figures -although the' census year was not a favourable one for that purpose in the west, and although two years has made a tremendous difference in the west, and although the next two years will make an equally great difference-I take the census figures and I find that west of Lake Superior, when this Bill becomes law, there will be twenty-eight constituencies. Winnipeg or the city of Winnipeg is to be one constituency, with a population of 42,314 ; the next largest in all that territory is Kootenay with a population of 31,952. In the province of Manitoba itself, where the redistribution should be a very simple matter, and where it can be very fairly and equally done as there are ten seats with a good unit, and there are no natural boundaries or traditions to respect, there are two constituencies, which added together, give a total population of one thousand less than this one constituency of Winnipeg. There is no reason why, in making up the constituencies, one should be given a smaller population than another-much less that the constituencies should be so arranged that two men in the city should have only the

same representation in this House as one man in the country. This Bill, on the face of It, tells us that there has been special treatment for the west because of its rapidly increasing population. The territories, not being provinces, can be dealt with by this parliament as they should be dealt with -given representation anticipating the increase of population that is now taking place ; and they are given ten members. I am aware that nothing of that kind can be done in the province of Manitoba. But 1 do submit, seeing that the principle of arbitrarily dealing with this matter has been recognized in the west, that the one city of the prairies should not be specially discriminated against in the opposite manner, that it should not be left with a less representation than it is entitled to to-day; and, with the prospect of increase of population before it for the next ten years, it should not be left represented here during that time by only one man. I do not wish to exaggerate in any way the prospective growth of that city. But it is absolutely fair to say that, if it increases in anything like the ratio of its increase since the census was taken, inside of three years it will be the third city of this Dominion in point of population. Judged by every other statistical standard than that of population, it is the third city in Canada to-day. The Minister of Customs can tell you that; the Postmaster General can tell you that; the Finance Minister, to whom the returns of the banks are sent, can tell you that; the keepers of the figures with regard to total trade can tell you that. And, inside of three years, even though its increase in population be not nearly so great as it has been for the last two years, it will be the third city in Canada in respect of population also. It has been represented by a delegate from the city council of Winnipeg, who was sent to Ottawa this week, that the population of the city of Winnipeg is nearer 70,000 than 60,000. I am not going to give that figure as authentic, because no municipal census has been taken since last winter. But I will give you facts which, I believe, prove conclusively that the population of Winnipeg at the end of last winter was not less than 54,000-and remember that since then there has been a tremendous immigration. The Dominion census reports of 1891 give the population of Winnipeg as 25,639. I take the municipal census for the same year and find that it gives the population as 27,068. So, there is a discrepancy of about 1,500 between the official Dominion census and the municipal census. The city takes a census every year. In 1901 the population of Winnipeg, according to the municipal census, was 44,778, and, according to the official Dominion census, 42,340, a discrepancy of a little over 2,000. This shows that both censuses, each on its
own lines, are taken properly and regularly, the proportion of discrepancy being about the same. Now, if we take the municipal census of 1902, the population was 48,411. In 1903, last winter, according to the municipal census, the population of the city was 56,741. There has been about the increase we might have expected, showing that there has been no attempt to pad the figures. Allowing for the discrepancy between the Dominion and municipal censuses, we find that if the Dominion census had been taken last winter it would have shown a population in Winnipeg of not less than 54,000. Although I recognize the fact that no extra representation can be given to Winnipeg because of its growth since the census, or its prospective growth between now and the next census, I claim that this rapid growth on the part of the city makes it all the more our duty not to discriminate against Winnipeg by giving it less representation than it is entitled to even on the basis of the census of 1901. I find that in discussing this matter of the cities with regard to the other provinces, it was pointed out that additional representation could not be given to tlie cities because the representation of the provinces was being cut down. For instance, in Ontario it was pointed out that the province was losing six members, and it was hard enough to cut these off; but if it was proposed that the rural constituencies should be still further reduced in order to increase the representation of the cities, the people would not stand it. It was said : If we are to increase the representation of the city tell us what constituencies in the rural districts we are to drop out. There is some force in that. I would not respect it to any great length myself, but I cannot deny that there is some force in it. But that argument does not apply to Manitoba, for the committee have to give three additional members to the province of Manitoba. And it would have been not only easy but fair, and not only fair, but absolutely the only way of being fair, to give to the city one of these three members, and to the rest of the province the other two. As I have said, in that province there are no traditions to be cousi ler-ed, no old established lines to be respected, no people who have been accustomed for long to see constituencies with certain bounds. We expect, in a redistribution, to see old lines completely wiped out. Conditions change so rapidly that we have not yet set up the boundaries which are to exist for any length of time. So, I claim that if the hon. member of the committee who spoke of his wishing that Winnipeg could have two members, had expressed that wish in the committee with any fervency at all, this additional member would have been given to Winnipeg. And no other constituency would have been trea bed wrong-

ly thereby nor would any have been deprived, of a fair share of representation.
Now, as I mentioned in reply to the hon. member for Saskatchewan, (Mr. Davis) not only have we nearly twice as large a population as the other constituencies of the province. but it must be remembered that the population in the rural constituencies includes Indians, who do not count on the voting strength, because the Indian is not a citizen, but a ward of the government. Of course he counts in the population, which includes all living persons; but for electoral purposes the Indian does not count. Therefore their number should be deducted from the population of the province when you are considering the representation of the province. At all events, seeing that they are all living in the country and not in the city, you simply increase the amount of unfairness by still allotting all the increased representation to the rural districts and not to the city of Winnipeg. If there were any prospect at all of getting justice, I would move an amendment, but I am not in the habit of moving amendments merely for the fun of the thing. But on behalf of the city of Winnipeg I do most earnestly protest against the redistribution of seats in Manitoba. I do it altogether irrespective of who represents that city at the present time, or who may represent it in the future. I would deal with this whole question of redistribution from Halifax to Vancouver, altogether irrespective of the gentlemen who are now representing the constituencies, and whether it would increase or decrease their chances of re-election. In redistributing the constituencies and in passing election laws we should have exclusively in view the trust we have here from the people so to arrange these things that they may send exactly whom they please to Ottawa. The people c>f Winnipeg think they are being unfairly dealt [DOT]with. I am not interested myself as to who they are going to send to Ottawa the next time. I hope they will send the person that the majority of the people freely choose to send. But I claim that according to all the canons of justice, according to right and the evidence that should enter into the consideration of a redistribution of seats, the people of Winnipeg are entitled to send two members to the next Dominion parliament.

speechtext:
So far as the province of Nova Scotia is concerned, the redistribution involved the loss of two members. There was no difference of opinion in the committee with respect to the place Where the loss of one member should fall.
The population of the different counties indicated very distinctly that the county of Pictou, under this redistribution, must lose one member. With reference to the disposition of the remaining counties of the province, no question arose except with regard to the three counties of Cape Breton, Victoria and Richmond. A majority of the committee thought that the county of Cape Breton should he divided, and that a portion of that county should be joined to the county of Victoria for the purpose of constituting an electoral district, and that the remainder of the county should form another electoral district. I was very much opposed to a division of the county of Cape Breton. The only alternative seemed to be to join the county of Victoria to the county of Richmond and to constitute them one electoral district. The matter was discussed more or less in the committee, and eventually the majority of the committee adhered to the conclusion at which they had first arrived. The county of Cape Breton in 1891 had a population, if I remember correctly, of about 34,000. Two members were given to that county at that time. Those members were awarded to the county of Cape Breton on account not only of its increasing population, but of its great commercial importance. It is a county in which very large coal mines are situated, and which has great commercial interests.

Particularly is that true, in view of the fact that gentlemen living in the county of Cape Breton, irrespective of their political associations, are firmly of the opinion that to-day, when we are making this redistribution, its population is something like 60,000. My hon. friends from Cape Breton, who are more familiar with the matter than I am, corroborate this statement. Some gentlemen

who are not extravagant in tlieir statements of facts of this kind, have gone so far as to state that the county of Cape Breton has at the present time a population nearer 70,000 than 60,000. Surely if a population of 31,000 in 1881 entitled the county of Cape Breton, with its great commercial interests, to two representatives in parliament, a population of 49,166 in 1901, or a population of from 60,000 to 70,000 at the present time, is entitled to the same representation.
But the county of Cape Breton has not that representation. Although its population has increased to 60,000 it does not have even the same representation because you are to have added to it the county of Victoria with a population of 10,571 and you are to give to the county of Cape Breton, with that enormously increased population and with the population of Victoria added to it, only the same representation in this parliament as was given to the county of Cape Breton when it had a population of 31,000. I regard that as a very extraordinary arrangement and indeed it is one in which I am not disposed to concur. The county of Cape Breton has not only an enormously increased population, but it has at the present time vastly more extended commercial interests than it ever had before ; it has these great coal companies and this enormous steel industry operating within its boundaries and it has at the present time I believe an electoral list of some 16,000 or 17,000 voters. My hon. friends from Cape Breton who are much more familiar with the situation there than I am will correct me in that if I am mistaken. I understood that the electoral list at the present time was somewhere in the vicinity of 16,000. Is there any justification under these circumstances for reducing the representation of the county of Cape Breton in that way ? Now, What had you as an alternative ? I admit that the alternative suggested in the committee is one that is not free from difficulties. It is to join together the county of Victoria and the county of Richmond. Certainly so far as population is concerned that is a much more equitable division. The population of the connty of Cape Breton, according to the census, is 49,166 people ; according to the estimates of my hon. friend from Cape Breton it is at least 60.000 people and giving it two representatives you will have, according to the census figures, one representative for every 24.500 people, or according to the present estimated population, one representative for every 30,000 of this population. .Toining together the counties of Richmond and Victoria you have in Richmond a population of 13,515, and you have iu Victoria a population of 10,571. making a total population for these two counties of 24.086. concerned there can be no question at all, the only question is whether there is, on account of the absence of direct contiguity between Victoria and Richmond any such reason as would override the considerations to which I have already referred. I believe that it is a better proposition in the interests of the province of Nova Scotia, in the interests of the people of Cape Breton, in the interests even of the people of Richmond and Victoria, to join the counties of Richmond and Victoria into one electoral division than to add the county of Victoria to the county of Cape Breton and to divide that united county into two electoral divisions. glad indeed if I could have sufficient order in the Committee to make myself heard, other wise I shall have to move that the Committee rise and that we adjourn the proceedings until we get sufficient order to be heard.
