maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I am not very familiar with the distances, but I suppose that the narrowest part would be from West Bay across to MacKinnon's' Harbour, say twelve or fifteen miles. The only communication between the county of Victoria and the county of Richmond is by the line of steamers that runs from Bad-declc and through the Grand Narrows to St. Peter's canal. From St. Peter's canal to Grand Narrows would be 25 to 30 miles. While I am on my feet, I may be permitted to say that with nearly everything that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) has said with regard to this proposition I agree. Like him, I am opposed to tile division of the county of Cape Breton. I would very much prefer that it should not be divided. There are several reasons why we should desire the situation to remain as it is. Unfortunately, however, the committee has seen fit to add the county of Victoria to the county of Cape Breton. Two propositions were available in joining Cape Breton and Victoria. One was to divide the united counties into two ridings, and the other was to have two members returned at large, as is at present the case in Cape Breton. There are some reasons, perhaps, why this latter should be done; but there are also reasons against it. I suppose there are but few in this House acquainted with that country, but those who are acquainted with it know that Victoria and Cape Breton united make a very large ter-

ritory, covering an extreme length, I suppose, of 125 or 150 miles. For my part, I regard that as too large a territory; and my own judgment led me to believe that if the county of Victoria were to be attached to Cape Breton it would be better for several reasons, that the united counties should be divided into ridings. I need not submit to the Committee what my reasons were. 1 do not know that it would be of very much interest to the Committee. But my judgment is that the interests of that territory would be much better maintained by having it divided rather than by having it as one constituency returning two members. I agree that there is no justification, so far as the matter of population is concerned, for any interference with Cape Breton, I fully agree with that part of the proposition of the leader of the opposition. Cape Breton county has made rapid strides in population since 1901, and it is making rapid strides to-day. But there were reasons- and the hon. leader of the opposition has suggested reasons-in opposition to the joining of the counties of Victoria aiid Richmond. Those of us who are acquainted with those counties must at once admit that there is absolutely no community of interest whatever between them. A good deal has been made of this matter of community of Interest, and I am willing to admit that there is a good deal in it. I am not prepared to shut my eyes to the fact that the county of Victoria has very strong views on that question. I am not prepared to shut my eyes to the fact that it is of importance to recognize what the views of the county of Victoria are. I know that the people of the county of Victoria, recognizing that the county had to be disturbed, preferred that It should be joined to Cape Breton, because their business interests are almost entirely with the county of- Cape Breton. The county of Cape Breton and the county of Victoria, for many years, have had close business communication. While I regret-and while I have very good reasons to regret-the fact that Victoria is being joined to Cape Breton, and that relations existing for so many years are about to be disturbed, I am bound to recognize the fact that it is, perhaps, the very best way out of the difficulty. The hon. leader of the opposition has suggested that certain conditions which existed in ihe county of Cape Breton for many years must be disturbed. I do not apprehend any difficulty on that score. So far as the religious question in Cape Breton is concerned, I do not think that that is a question that will be a serious one to either county. I am satisfied that that question will work itself out all right. There is a good deal of difference of opinion, no doubt. It may well happen, and I have no doubt it will happen, that quite a number of people will be dissatisfied. So far as my political party Mr. JOHNSTON (Cape Breton).
is concerned, it will certainly not receive any advantage, nor will this arrangement work to the advantage of myself as a politician. At the same time, I recognize that it is the best that could be made under the circumstances. Both political parties in the county of Cape Breton agree in attaching no significance, from a party point of view, to the division. The leading organ of the Conservative party in my county was one of the earliest to suggest this division, and has supported it. I have only to reiterate that I would have been much better pleased if the committee had seen its way to leave Cape Breton undisturbed; at the same time, I do not shut my eyes to the fact that there were difficulties in the way of accepting the proposition which was submitted by the leader of the opposition.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
The ground of the difference as respects the redistribution in the province of Nova Scotia is really very small, and I am glad to say that it has really no political significance whatever. We agree in the first place that Nova Scotia must lose two members ; there is no dispute over that. We agree that one of them shall be taken from the county of Pictou. That county has for some years had a smaller population than the county of Cumberland, yet Pictou has had two members while Cumberland had only one ; therefore it goes without saying that one of the two members should be taken from Pictou. That brings us to the consideration of the second member to be withdrawn from Nova Scotia. The leader of the opposition and myself agree that that second member should be taken from the eastern portion of the province which forms the island of Cape Breton. There was a time when Cape Breton and Nova Scotia were spoken of as two separate places. Even now on the island of Cape Breton a man will ask you if you come from Nova Scotia, and vice versa. The island of Cape Breton may be spoken of as a unit. Now, we find that it includes the four counties of Inverness, Richmond, Cape Breton and Victoria, having by the last census a population of 97,695, a little less than the number which will be required to qualify by the general rule for a membership of four. The island of Cape Breton now has five, and inasmuch as under the figures I have quoted it would only have a population,' for less than four members, no injustice will be done that portion of Nova Scotia by assigning it four members instead of five. They will still be represented rather above than below their proper proportion. So we agree that one member must be taken from Pictou, and that the second must be taken from the island of Cape Breton.
That brings us to the final point as to which county in Cape Breton shall be subject to readjustment, and there again we agree, because my hon. friend the leader

of the opposition and myself agree that the county which is to be operated upon must be the county of Victoria. It is the smallest constituency in Nova Scotia, and having resolved that one member must be taken from the island of Cape Breton, it is most natural that we should agree that the smallest county in the island should be taken as the subject for consideration. So that brings us down to the single question of the distribution we are to make as respects the county of Victoria. We both agree that the county of Victoria must be dealt with ; the next question is to what neighbouring county you will attach it. I would have to agree at once with the leader of the opposition if population only had to be considered. Richmond has a population of 13,515, and Victoria a population of 10,571. United, their population is only 24,086, something below the unit to secure one member. Therefore the union which my hon. friend would propose to make of these two counties1 would seem to be quite equitable, and if we had to consider nothing but population, I would have to agree at once with the proposal of my hon. friend ns fair and reasonable. But against that there is that question which has so often been referred to during the debate, but which in no case could lie so well referred to as in this case, the question of community of interest. There is really no community of interest between the two counties that my hon. friend wishes to unite. As has been pointed out here by the bon. member for Richmond (Mr. Mathesou), they are separated by the waters of the Bras d'or lake, and there is no regular line of communication which leads the people of one county to visit the other. There is practically very little communication between these counties, although they both lie in the island of Cape Breton. So strong is that the case, that I am inclined to think that nobody in the county of Richmond wants to be united with Victoria, and I think that nobody in Victoria wants to be united with the county of Richmond. The division which my hon. friend proposes would actually please nobody in the two! counties that he would unite.
Well, if there is not a community of interest, if there are not those conditions which we are all disposed to recognize as important in considering the union of two counties, then we are forced to look at the question to see how we can dispose of Victoria county otherwise. Now, I have prepared here two maps which illustrate the matter. In this map are shown the constituencies as the committee propose to arrange them. We take he county of Cape Breton ancl the county of Victoria and unite them ; but finding them too large for one constituency, as they cover a very large territory, finding the travel difficult, finding they could not reasonably be kept together as one constituency, we then take what seems to be a
fair line of division. You will observe that the portion to the right represented in the one colour is a compact mass. There can be no question there of taking out of one county a municipality or township and adding it to another ; it is a solid compact constituency. Then above you find also a solid compact constituency projecting away to Cape North. Here also you are not cutting out one place and associating it with some other place ; there is a solid compact mass forming one constituency, and a solid compact mass forming another. Therefore there will be no difficulty whatever on geographical lines in justifying the division suggested by these circumstances.
Now, let me show the division as proposed by the leader of the opposition. He proposes to create a county by uniting the two counties of Richmond and Victoria. This map does not show, as hon. gentlemen might suppose, in yellow, two separate constituencies. These two yellow patches form the one constituency under the proposition of the leader of the opposition. They are wide apart and separated by the waters of the Bras d'Or lake. They do not touch each other at any point. They are actually separate units, separated by the waters of the Bras d'Or lake, and there is an entire absence of that connection and community of interest which we all recognize as desirable to bring about if possible. For these reasons, if it be admitted that down to that point my hon. friend and myself agree, if it be admitted that the county of Victoria must be dealt with, then we are reduced to this question, whether we will unite Vic-t toria with the county of Cape Breton or whether we will unite it with a county which is separated entirely from it by the waters of the Bras d'Or lake.
We think from every point of view that it is better to unite the county of Victoria with the county of Cape Breton, which lies alongside of it than to unite it with the county of Richmond, which is near the southern part of Cape Breton and which is separated in such a marked manner from Victoria by the waters of the lake. Then, in addition to that there is the fact that as stated by the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Johnston) there is a very close relation between the people of the county of Victoria and the people of the county of Cape Breton. The island of Boularderie in the Bras d'Or lake is partly in Cape Breton and partly in Victoria, .and in travelling through there one hardly knows whether he is in North Sydney, which as a thriving and growing town, may almost be looked upon as the commercial capital of Victoria county. There is more natural communication and more trade between Victoria and North Sydney than there is certainly with any other portion of Nova Scotia. I think that the geographical difficulties in the way of the proposition of the hon. leader of the opposition are therefore very considerable.

In addition to the geographical advantages, there is the argument of the community of interest and there is the further fact, that, far from the matter being regarded as in any sense political, the leading organ of the Conservative party in the county has recognized that this is a fair and proper division that the committee suggest. Having agreed then, as we do, that it is necessary to unite the county of Victoria with the county of Cape Breton, we then proceeded to divide them so that we might make two convenient constituencies. Here again we have an easy line of division. The waters of Sydney ' harbour and of East Bay suggest a line of division which is a very natural one. On one side we have North Sydney and Sydney Mines, both thriving and growing towns ; on the south side we get the old town of Sydney and Glace Bay, in the centre of the great coal mining region of Cape Breton, and from that you have the southern district running to Louisburg. 1 think the division which has been proposed lays down a fair and natural line whereby the large population of this section is associated with the territory with which it is naturally in communication, where all its trade and all its tastes and inclinations lie. There is no politics in it. I think for that and other reasons which I have ventured to present, that the proposition which the committee have agreed to has more merit in it than that which the hon. leader of the opposition has made, though I am bound to admit that in point of population alone the union of the two counties which he has mentioned would seem to be a solution of the matter. But, inasmuch as there are other difficulties, I think the weight of evidence is In favour of the report of the majority of the committee. As to what I may call the religious side of the Question, which has been referred to by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, that is a matter which should never be entirely lost sight of, but I have enough confidence in the good spirit which prevails in those counties to believe that the question will settle itself. I must remind my hon. friend that although, as he says, a rule prevails elsewhere whereby it is supposed that both of the great denominations secure representation, it does not always work out in that way. On two or three occasions we have found that the results did not, come about. I have a strong hope that under the rearrangement of these constituencies the different religious bodies will be as well represented as in other constituencies where special arrangements have not produced the results expected. As respects the province of Nova Scotia, the division between the two parties on this question of redistribution is excedingly small and I rejoice to say that there is no political significance in this arrangement, because I do not think anybody can state that tbis is giving a political advantage to one party or the other. Tak-Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
ing all these things into consideration, I think the report of the majority of the committee is one which would commend itself to the committee, and which will find favour in the province of Nova Scotia.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The lion. Minister of Finance has referred to a great many matters which I did not bring before tlie committee at all. I was not suggesting that if you add Victoria to Gape Breton the proposed division of the united counties	is a bad one.	I	have not considered that at all. I have had no intimation that it is. I do not know whether it is a	good one	or not.	At	all events I didnot	refer to	it. I	did	not suggest inany way, although any hon. friend lias laid a great deal of stress on the point, that there has been a political motive In doing what has been done. I was not suggesting that, but I was alluding to the vex-y unfortunate result as far as Cape Breton is concerned, and I can emphasize that further by pointing out that under tlie proposed redistribution 70,000 of a population in Cape Breton and	Victoria	will return	two representatives to parliament, while 13,515 people in Richmond will return one.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: AVill the hon. gentleman tell me why we have had in the past, 74,000 people in the county of Halifax returning two members, and 10,000 people in the county of Richmond returning one member ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I am aware of that, and I pointed that out before tbis Committee, and before tlie committee to which this Bill was confided. That is a condition of affairs which perhaps will have to be remedied at the first opportunity. Tlie distinction is that in this case you are not continuing that condition of affairs, but you are creating that condition of affairs. Cape Breton, with 31.000, returned two representatives, again in 1891, with 34,000, it returned two representatives. It has increased its population, according to tlie census of 1901, to 48,000, and the hon. member for Cape Breton says that at the present time it has a population of 60,000. Then you bring in 10,000 more people, by bringing in another county, and you give both counties combined with a population of 70,000, two representatives. In addition to that you give the comity of Richmond, with 13,000 people, one representative. That is to say, that 35,000 people In the combined counties of Victoria and Cape Breton have the same weight in this parliament as 13,000 people in the county of Richmond. I do not disguise the fact that there are practical difficulties In the way of uniting tlie counties of Richmond and Victoria. I said that this was the choice of two evils, hut it seems to me that in view of the enormous disproportion in the population it would be better to join Richmond with Vic-

toria than to minimize the representation of Cape Breton to the extent to which it is proposed to do. A great deal of stress has been laid upon the lack of community of interest and of communication. In one sense there is a difficulty in that regard, but possibly there is as good communication between Richmond and Victoria as there is between the eastern and western parts of my own constituency, a constituency extending for more than 140 miles along the coast line, with no railway running between the east and the. west so that the people in the eastern part of the county, 140 miles away from the western part of the county, have practically no means of communicating with each other except by water. There is no regular liue of steamers. As far as that is concerned, it is exactly in the same position as Richmond and Victoria. There is, of course, a steamer which runs from Halifax and calls at some points on the eastern coast, but there is no steamer running from points on the eastern coast to points on the western coast that I am aware of in the county of Halifax. Any person iu the western part of the county of Halifax has to travel over 100 miles by stage or wagon to communicate with people in the opposite part of the constituency, or else he must communicate solely by water. It is not an absolutely conclusive argument that the Minister of Finance has made in that regard, although I appreciate most fully what he has said. I admit that it is a choice of two evils, but I do not think these two evils stand in regard to each other exactly in the light that my hon. friend has presented to the House. The Great Bras D'Or Lake does not divide the communities of Richmond and Victoria at all times of the year ; it affords an easy means of communication between them during a great many months. As to the community of interest, I understand that the people of Richmond and Victoria counties, follow for the most part agricultural and fishing pursuits, and that there is community of interest-in the sense we have been discussing it-to a large extent. I do not deny that so far as business relations are concerned, these would be closer between Victoria and the north part of Cape Breton, than between Victoria and Richmond, although I am not prepared to admit that no business relations exist between the people of Victoria and of Richmond. I am not persuaded, even by the pertinent remarks of the Finance Minister, that the right choice has been made between the two evils, because I do regard it as a discre,-pancy that almost shocks our sense of what is right, to give to this great county of Cape Breton and Victoria, witli a population of 70,000 at the present time, merely two representatives in parliament, while the county of Richmond with a population of only 13,000 returns one. I am not saying that of course as iu any way reflecting upon
the county of Richmond, which is inhabited by a thriving, progressive, industrious and enterprising people. I am merely dealing with the great discrepancy of population between the constituencies.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I admit that this arrangement is not very satisfactory. I may say to the leader of the opposition, that we had three choices. One was : Whether we should unite Victoria county with the northern part of Inverness, and Richmond with the southern part of Inverness. That proposition would not be acceptable to the people in any of these counties.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I do not think that was ever mentioned in the committee.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I am glad that the leader of the opposition takes such a moderate view of the case. I, for one, would have been very pleased if Richmond and Victoria were united, but since this met with opposition from Liberals and Conservatives alike in each county, and as there is no community of interest between the two, I think the arrangement made is perhaps better. Twelve or fifteen miles of water separate the two counties; the county town of each county is separated by 40 miles of water, and on land they are more than 50 miles apart, and the greater portion of the territory lying between is sparsely settled. During the winter there is practically no communication between the two. Speaking from the Cape Breton standpoint, I believe that the county of Cape Breton will have as much influence in representation as it has had in the past. I look upon it, that the county of Cape Breton having absorbed Victoria county, the community of interest between the two is so strong, that the county which I have had for a short time the honour of representing, will not suffer on account of the absorption of some
10,000	more population. On the contrary, I look forward with hope, that after the next census is taken, the fact that we have absorbed Victoria county will enable us to have not only three members, but probably four members. As regards . the religious complexion of the county of Cape Breton, I have not the slightest doubt that in the future as in the past, an arrangement will be come to in that regard, and that there will be no greater difficulty in the matter than heretofore.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I merely mentioned that point because I understood that there was that custom or tradition in the county of Cape Breton, and that this union of the counties was somewhat likely to interfere with it. I am willing to accept most fully, upon that point, tire assurance given by my hon. friends from Cape Breton, that they do not think any difficulty will be experienced in that regard in the future.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I wish to point out that there is no communication either in

summer or in winter, between Richmond and Victoria, unless a man takes a boat of bis own. The steamer leaving St. Peters does not touch Victoria county at all. There is no community of interest whatever between the two counties.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
The remarks of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition would convey the impression that the county of Cape Breton will be under represented in this parliament. The hon. gentleman in speaking of the population of Cape Breton county, always refers to its supposed population at present, and when referring to the other counties he takes the census returns. We must be fair. This redistribution is based upon the census of 1901, and some portion of the great progress of Cape Breton county had taken place prior to that census. In 1891 the population of Cape Breton county was 34,000, and at last census it was 49,000. As to how much the county of Cape Breton has increased in population since the taking of last census, is, I suppose a matter of controversy. There are many communities which claim a population greater than that which the census gives, but time does not always vindicate the claim. However, I hope that the most optimistic view as to Cape Breton county will be fully realized. Whether or not the population is 60,000 today is not the question. We must take into consideration the census returns which gives a population of 49,000. The leader of the opposition says that it is rather a' shock to have the 59,000 people of Cape Breton and Victoria with only two members, while the county of Richmond with 10,000 will have one member. It ought not be so great a shock, because for many years the county of Halifax, with 74,000 population in the last census, has had only two members, while the county of Victoria with a population of
10,000	has had one. There are anomalies of that kind which we cannot hope to cure. I do not agree with my hon. friend that we are creating new difficulties because we are giving two members to Cape Breton and Victoria with a population of 59,000, while Cumberland and Pictou, with a combined population of 69,000, have only two members. Therefore I do not think that Cape Breton is under represented at all; but I have strong hope that, with the great growth which we all expect is going to take place in Cape Breton, when the next redistribution occurs we shall be able to give that county for itself two members or more. 1 feel very hopeful that, through that and other agencies, the maritime provinces will by that time recover some of the lost ground, and that, instead of taking members from them, we may add something to their representation.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Either Cape Breton is under represented now, or it has been very much over represented in the past.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Unquestionably it has been.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I'do not know whether my hon. friends from Cape Breton will be inclined to agree with that. I do not think there has been any impression in the province of Nova Scotia during the last ten years that the county of Cape Breton has been over represented in this parliament. If there lias been any such impression, I have not heard of it up to the present time.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: We will still have two members.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I am aware of that. But if, with a population of 34,000 people, it was not over represented surely, when its population has increased to 49,000, according to the census, or 60,000 according to the statement of my hon. friend, when it is joined to another county, and it still has only retained its original representation, it is under represented.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: On the question of over representation of the county of Cape Breton, it is true nobody has complained of it. Yet here is the fact chat the county of Cumberland, with a population according to the census of 1891, of 34,529, had one member, while Cape Breton, with a population of 34,234, had two members. I do not think it is wrong, in the face of that, to say that the county of Cape Breton, proportionately, was over represented. But its over representation came about at an earlier stage. If it had been repress lied according to the census of 1891, it would not have been given two members; but it had got them long before that, and it was not thought wise to disturb them. With the inequalities which we have in Nova Scotia, some of the counties have 33,000 or 34,000, while others have 10,000 or 11,000, and yet no man would undertake to say that these small counties should lose their representatives. We have to submit to these anomalies, and make the best of them.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I suppose the second representative was given to Cape Breton, in the first instance, on account of the great commercial interests centred in that county ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I think the second member was given in 1872, when the coal business in that county perhaps did not amount to over 200,000 or 300,000 tons per annum.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: What was the reason, then, of the second representative ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Another member was to be given to Nova Scotia, and Cape Breton happened to be one of the largest counties. I am not prepared to say that it was not fair and just to give the county the additional member, although

there were people who felt that on the ground of its commercial importance Halifax was entitled to the additional member.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: There is some discrepancy in the population still. I observe that South Cape Breton will have a population of 35,000, while North Cape Breton and Victoria will have a population of 24,650, a discrepancy of about 10,000. Both north and south Cape Breton are likely rapidly to increase in population, and the discrepancy will probably continue. In North Cape Breton there are North Sydney and Sydney Mines, two very growing places, and in South Cape Breton there are the town of Sydney and Glace Bay. It would seem as if there might have been a better division made, so far as population is concerned. The difference, amounting to 10,000, is equal to the whole population of Victoria, which is now added to Cape Breton. While there is, I admit, a very good geographical line laid out by East Bay and the waters of Sydney Harbour, it would have been as well perhaps to have endeavoured to equalize the population to a greater extent, which I think could have been done without a great deal of difficulty.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
The inequality of population to which my kon. friend refers is undoubtedly considerable, and it would be well, if possible, to avoid it; but that community of interest which we have talked about seems to outweigh other considerations. My own knowledge of the county is not perhaps greater than that of my hon. friend; but I am advised that none of these districts could be moved from one constituency to the other in a way to be satisfactory to the people. The community of interest makes the old shire town of Sydney the natural centre of the one, and North Sydney the natural centre of the other.

On item, New Brunswick-the city and county of St. John.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I wish to say a word with reference to the proposed redistribution of constituencies in the province of New Brunswick, as it interests me somewhat intimately, from the fact that by the addition of the county of Albert to the county of King's a new constituency ik formed. Unfortunately, the population of the province of New Brunswick has not increased during the last decade proportionately to that of the province of Quebec, which forms the basis of representation, and therefore it has to lose one member. Now, the county of King's has very nearly the unit of population. The unit is about 25,000, while the population of King's is somewhat in excess of 21.000. It is proposed to add to the 370 *
county of King's the county of Albert, with a population in round numbers of ll,000r which will give to the united counties a population of about 32,000. Now, there are other counties in the province of New Brunswick with a population less than that of King's. For instance, the county of Res-tigouche has a population of 13,000. The county of St. John has a population of about 10,000, and yet it is proposed to give it a member. Indeed, it is proposed to give to the city of St. John one member, as it has at present, and to give to the city and county of St. John another member, which practically means giving two members to the city of St. John. I think it has been laid down as a principle by hon. gentlemen opposite, in connection with this redistribution of seats, that urban constituencies should not have the same proportionate representation as rural constituencies.
That is the excuse that is given for allowing to the great city of Montreal only six members and to the great city of Torpnto only five members, making a unit of some
42,000	to 43,000 to each representative. In the city of St. John we find that this principle does not apply ; that city is to have two members for a population of 40,000, yet in the city and county of Halifax there is a total population of 74,000, and they have only two members. In St. John, however, we find two representatives for about 50,000 people, really two representatives for that city of 40,000 population. Here we have the great county of Westmoreland, the largest county in the province, with a population of 43,000, and only one representative, although it is a rural constituency, and yet the city of St. John, an urban constituency, has two representatives, because you cannot get away from the fact that although for the second member that is given to the city of St. John the county of St. John is added with its 10,000 population, these two members are really representatives of the city of St. John, because the people of the city of St. John vote for the second representative, and being so largely in the majority, 40,000 to 10,000, that member is practically a member for the city of St. John. Therefore you are giving two members to a population of 40,000, a unit of 20,000. Yet the county of Westmoreland which contains a city of 10,000 and has a total population of 42,000, has only one member. If you unite the county of Albert and the county of King's, you will have a population of 32,000. It would be fair for the county of St. John aijd fair for the county of Albert if we should unite these two ; that would give you a population well under the unit of population of 21,000. We have heard a great deal about community of interest, and I suppose it will be contended that there is absolutely no community of interest between, Albert and St. John and that there is a close community between



Albert and King's. I am as familiar with all three of these counties as any member of this House, and I say that there is as much community of interest between the county of Albert and the county of St. John as between the county of Albert and the county of King's. The county of St. John and the county of Albert are both coast counties lying along the coast of the Bay of Fundy ; they abut upon each other and there is a greater length of the east line of the county of St. John abutting on the west line of the county of Albert than there is of the east line of the county of King's on the west line of the county of Albert. It is true that for judicial purposes these two counties are joined, tout what community of interest does joining two counties for judicial purposes create ? There is absolutely no trade between the people of the county of Albert and the people of the county of King's ; they are as distinct and separate in trade matters as Restigouche and Victoria. Whatever trading outside of their own county the people of Albert do, is with the people of the county of Westmoreland, which lies west of them, but with which they cannot be united on account of the large population of Westmoreland, and with the city of St. John and not with King's. If a man goes as far as Sussex, which is the principal town in my constituency of King's, he will go on to St. John and do his trading at the commercial capital of the province. That is what, as a matter of fact, is done except by a few persons who do a little trading between Elgin and Sussex there is absolutely no trade between Albert and King's. Hon. gentlemen from New Brunswick are familiar with the geography of that province and they know that this proposed constituency of King's and Albert will be a constituency about 140 miles long, whereas by uniting St. John and Albert you would get a much shorter constituency. Therefore, it seems to me that it is my duty to point out to this committee the wrong that is toeing inflicted on the people of Albert and King's by this iniquitous gerrymander in that province. From every consideration the proper thing to do would be to unite the county of Albert with the county of St. John, unless you were to adopt the plan which has been suggested of breaking up the county of St. John. There is a sort of division in the county of St. John between the eastern and western part of the county of St. John, and we might attach one portion of that county say to the county of Albert and attach the other to the county of King's. That might be done, but of course in that way you would have to break the county boundaries, which might be a; sort of wrench to hon. gentlemen opposite. I do not suggest that, because I believe you have laid down the principle that you must not interfere with county boundaries. It would be very easy were it not for that

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: principle which has been established and carried out so far as Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick are concerned, but which I understand has been deviated from in Ontario to make a very, fair division, by breaking up the county of St. John. I suppose the hon. gentleman who represents the county of St. John does not see that matter in the same light as I do. But the proper, the fair and reasonable way, if you do not want to break the county boundaries, is to unite the county of Albert and the county of St. John. In this way you would give to St. John the same unit of population as is given to Toronto and Montreal, 40,000 to one member, and you would not have the anomaly of the county of Albert, with a population of 11,000, lying right alongside the county of Westmoreland with a population of 42,000. This would occur by uniting the county of St. John and the county of King's, but as I have said, the proper way would be to unite the county of Albert with the county of St. John, giving a population of 21,000, and giving thei city of St. John one member to 42,000 population. That is the urban unit of representation, and it seems to me that would be a fair way all around. King's would have a population of about 23,000. I bring this forward as showing the view I take, which, I think, is a fair and proper view of this matter.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I cannot help thinking that the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Fowler) language in discussing this question is strong out of all proportion to the reason and argument which he has presented to the committee. On what basis he feels justified in pronouncing this an iniquitous gerrymander, I am entirely at a loss to understand. He has not suggested any political advantage as being conferred upon one party or any political disadvantage thrust upon another. He has not suggested anything that would even lead one to suspect that any such consideration had influenced the committee in making this redistribution. I think it would be impossible for him to furnish data that would lead one to suspect in the remotest degree that the committee had been so influenced.
It became necessary, unfortunately, as the hon. member stated, to make provision for reducing the representation of New Brunswick in this parliament by one. How to bring that about we expected to find, and did find, attended with difficulties. How to bring that about has caused a good deg.1 of thought and study and consideration of the whole situation in the province. I myself have given a good deal of consideration to the matter. And, looking at the problem which we have to solve, I think it would be impossible to make any proposal that would be more equitable or would give more satisfaction to the people affected by it than the suggestion that has been made. Our object, in the first place,

was to adhere to county bounds-that was our controlling consideration. We could not break up constituencies, for such a course has not been taken in any previous redistribution of the province. When we came to consider which constituencies we should join together, there seemed a very limited held for the carrying out of what we had in view. There seemed to me at all events-and I am prepared to take my share of responsibility in connection with this redistribution-only two constituencies in the northern portion of the province and two in the southern portion which could be united. Restigouche might be annexed to Gloucester. Restigouche is a small county, and Restigouche and Gloucester together would not have a population very much larger, perhaps, than might be assigned as the unit of representation. But they are both growing counties, and the population of the two combined is very much larger than that of any other two counties that could possibly be proposed for union. The other two counties were Albert and King's. Restigouche, I may say has a population of 10,586, and Gloucester, 27,936, making a total population for these two counties of 38,522. The population of Albert is 10,925, and of Kng's, 22,655, a total for Albert and King's of 32,580, or about
6,000	less than the total population of Restigouche and Gloucester. So, if we were to unite two counties and not breaking county boundaries, there only remained possible to be united the counties-it appeared to me -of Albert and King's. And it so appeared to the committee. My hon. friend (Mr. Fowler) has asked, why not unite the county of St. John with the county of Albert ? For many reasons. They could not practically be united. It would not be agreeable to the people of either counties

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Yes, it would.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Well I know it would be entirely disagreeable to the people of the county of St. John. And I have not heard of there being any demand of any importance from the county of Albert that that county should.be united to the county of St. John.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Blair) permit me to ask him a question ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Has not the hon. gentleman received a communication from the local member for the county of Albert in favour of having the counties of Albert and St. John united rather than the counties of Albert and King's ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman means Mr. Osman, the member of the local legislature for the county ? I think that gentleman would very much desire that. But I do not see that any public op-
370*
inion on this subject exists behind him urging that that course should be taken ; and I think that if any strong feeling on that question existed it would have made itself felt before this. The proposal that the county of Albert should be united with the county of St. John is not a practical proposal. The two counties do not lie, in any real sense, contiguous. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) nods as if to say that they do. I still maintain the correctness of what I have said. A very remote portion of the county of Albert, far outside of the range of population, far away from the settled districts, does lie along side the end of the county of St. John. But to pass from one county to the other in that way, you go far away from the ordinary routes of travel. As anybody who knows that country is aware, you must pass through the woods, through an unsettled and unpeopled district in both counties. The people of the county of Albert who wish to go to the county of St. John or vice versa, in order to reach their destination would have to pass through the county of King's-from one end of the county of King's to the other. That is the only way they could go, unless they went by water, and there are no regular means of communication by that way. They would naturally pass along the Intercolonial Railway in the county of Albert and over the Albert County local road, the Salisbury and Harvey Railway. So, it must be self-; evident to anybody who knows the situation, that, to unite these two counties would be to bring together counties that are totally disconnected, and that to reach either from the other you would have to pass through the county of King's. Is that a reasonable or equitable suggestion ? Is that a suggestion that any committee dealing with a matter of this kind would put in operation ? I am strongly convinced it is not. On the contrary, the connection between the county of King's and the county of Albert is very close. The whole settled portion of both lie contiguous, and the people pass and repass over the line of railway which traverses the whole length of King's, and almost the entire length of Albert. Railway communication is close and regular, affording the best facilities for the people to come together. I do not know that they have any close business interests in common. You find in but few instances among rural constituencies that close business connections exist between them. Their connection is with the business centres outside. There are no business centres of any consequence in the county of King's. We admit that the people of the county of Albert would have business connection with St. John. There are no centres in the county of Albert with which the people of King's would have close business connection. But there is a possibility of communicating with each other by easy and speedy methods, to a greater extent possibly than would be the

case between the counties of St. John and Albert if they were united.
Now, my hon. friend says, why do you not break up the county of St. John ? Why are the city and county of St. John allowed to have! two representatives, particularly as the city vote is cast in the county proper, and the county vote is cast in the city proper ? I do not think that system! is an ideal one, but we are not disturbing existing conditions any more than is absolutely necessary. The city and county of St. John have a population of nearly 52,000, and two members do not seem to be an excessive number for a constituency of that population. Moreover, the people of the city and county of St. John are very well content with the existing arrangement and with the present representation. There is no complaint, therefore there is no reason why we should invite any controversy. Let well enough alone until there is a grievance, and if it is shown to exist it can be remedied. When we come to Westmoreland, we find it has a population of over 40,000, and it has only one member. I do not quite agtree that the county of Westmoreland can be classed as an exclusively rural population. The city of Moncton with a population of some 10,000 is in the county of Westmoreland.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I stated that.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Sackville is scarcely entitled to be spoken of as a rural population. Sackville is a large and flourishing town, and there are one or two other large and flourishing villages in the county. Therefore the population of Westmoreland cannot fairly be called a purely rural population. But my hon. friend would not suggest that.we should disturb the conditions in Westmoreland. There is no reason why the county of Albert should be added to the county of Westmoreland, there are no reasons why they should not be united. There are no reasons why conditions should be disturbed in St. John unless you could thereby increase the convenience to the people, and unless that was the only way in which you could provide for the contingency we are called upon to meet. I think myself that the committee have done well in adopting this method of solving the difficulty. I am quite sure it would be wholly impracticable to connect the counties of St. John and Albert. You would have to make a circuit of seventy or eighty miles after you left one county to get into the other. It is a proposition that the committee should not entertain. My hon. friend has not made any motion on the subject, but if he does I trust the committee will not entertain it.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
In order to go from Albert to King's it is necessary to go through the county1 of Westmoreland. The railway runs to Salisbury, and Salisbury is in the county of Westmoreland, and you have to Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
travel at least fifteen miles from Salisbury to Anagance before you get to the extreme end of the county of King's. In order to go from Albert to the extreme end of the county of King's by rail, you have first got to travel through the county of Albert, then through the county of Westmoreland, then through the county of King's and then through a portion of the county of St. John before you get to the extreme limit of the county of King's. So I think a gentleman who is a candidate would have to travel through Albert, through Westmoreland, through King's and through St. John to get to the parishes of Westfield and Greenwich in the county of King's, or a distance of about 140 miles in order to get to that part of the constituency as it is proposed here. Now the hon. gentleman says there is! no protest from the county of Albert against a union of that county with King's, or any request in favour of a union of Albert aud St. John. I am rather surprised that the hon. gentleman should speak in such slighting terms of the gentleman to whom I referred, and who, the hon. gentleman admitted, had made a strong protest against that union, and in favour of the other union. I had an idea that the hon. gentleman to whom I refer, the senior member of the county for the local legislature, was a man of some importance. He is certainly very popular in his own constituency, and I think if any man is authorized to speak for the county it is the hon. gentleman to whom I refer and who was elected recently by a large majority. Surely he is in a position to speak with some authority. I had a personal conversation with him. and he assured me that he and his Liberal friends in the county were very much opposed to the union of Albert with King's, and! would prefer a union with the county of St. John. Of course they would prefer to be left alone, I am sure that is the feeling in the county of King's, irrespective of party. Liberals and Conservatives of the county of King's would prefer to see the county remain as it is. But as we have to make a union somewhere, the people of Albert, the Liberals more particularly of the county of Albert, would prefer to be united with the county of St. John. I do not think the hon. gentleman has brought forward any reason to. show why that union should not take place. He says there has been no complaint among the people of St. John about the present redistribution. Why should the people of St. John complain ? They are being left just as they are, of course they would not complain. That is a peculiar sort of argument, and the hon. gentleman must be rather hard up to resort to it. As it is, the people of St. John are left with a representation considerably in excess of any other city of Canada. The city and the county taken together have a representation largely in excess of most of the rural constituencies

of Canada. Therefore there will naturally be no complaint on their part. In what I said with respect to breaking up a county, I did not put that forward as a proposition of my own, I said the suggestion had been made by the hon. gentleman in this House to break up the county of St. John. But, with this principle put forward which has been violated in some of the provinces and maintained in the maritime provinces it would prevent that being done. I think it is more important to give representation to the population than it is to maintain county boundaries. I fail to see why the breaking of county boundaries is a very serious matter. I think it is more important to carry out the principle of representation by population than that county boundaries shall be kept intact. I have .not moved a resolution in respect to this matter. I have no personal feeling against the people of Albert. On the contrary I have a friendly feeling towards them. I prefer, however, to be left alone.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: It is a painful necessity.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: It may be a painful necessity and the results may be very painful to me. I do not think that is the object of the hon. gentleman who arranged this redistribution. I do not insinuate that there1 was any such object although the hon. gentleman (Mr. Blair) seemed to suggest that it had been carried out on that line. I am making no insinuation that this was done for political purposes and I do not see why the hon. member for St. John made the statement he did as to that.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) referred to this particular arrangement as an iniquitous gerrymander. What did he have in his mind when he said that ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: In view of the fact that tlm city of St. John was having a representation in this House in excess of any city in Canada and in view of the fact that the county of St. John with 10,000 people would have just as much say as the counties of Albert and King's with 33.000 people and a^ Westmoreland with 42,000 people. I thought the arrangement was somewhat surprising but I never said a single word about the political significance of it. I avoided saving! anything about that.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: My hon. friend has made reference to one of the gentlemen! who represent Albert in the provincial House with the view of suggesting that I had cast some reflection upon him. I certainly would be very sorry to be understood as doing that, because Mr. Osman is a gentleman whom I respect very highly. He is a particular friend of my own and I would not think of treating his opinion lightly or of treating it with disrespect. All I intended to say was that there was no important exhibition of public opinion in the constituency.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Is the hon. gentleman not aware that the Liberal Association of Hillsborough, the principal town in Albert, met and passed a resolution condemning this redistribution V
Hon. Mr. BLAIR, No, I do not recall the fact.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: As I am informed it is a fact.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I am not aware that it is a fact.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I do not think it would be proper for any one to say that this is an iniquitous gerrymander, but I recognize the difficulties connected with the redistribution of New Brunswick. I do not personally view the arrangement of the committee as being an ideal one but I recognize that when you turn your eyes over the province of New Brunswick it would be almost impossible to unite any other two constituencies more favourably than you can unite these two. It would seem to me that an i leal arrangement as far as the situation in New Brunswick is concerned would be a division of the county of St. John. That county has about 10,000 inhabitants. It consists of four parishes, two on the western side of the harbour and two on the eastern side. These eastern parishes have about the same population as the western parishes. The eastern parishes are joined to the county of King's. They have about 5,000 inhabitants and it would seem to me that the proper union would be to join these two parishes with the county of King's which would make a constituency of about 26,000. The western parishes would be united to the county of Charlotte which would make a constituency of about the same number in population. I recognize, however,, that the principle laid down and adhered to very generally was that you should confine yourself to county boundaries and such being the case I recognize that it would be very inconsistent to make a change such as was proposed by myself or outlined in my remarks just now. The county of Albert is isolated. I quite agree with my hon. friend from St. John (Hon. Mr. Blair) that it would be almost impossible to unite Albert county with the county of St. John. There is an impenetrable barrier between these two counties such as he has described. They have not even highways communicating with each other and they only unite on the shore of the Bay of Fundy. There is no water communication, there would be very high hills and mountains to get over and therefore the difficulty described by the hon. member for King's. N.B. (Mr. Fowler) in respect to the people of Albert getting to the extreme western end of the county of King's would be only itensified by the union of the county of St. John with the county

of Albert because they would have to go away around by tbe several railroads passing through the entire length of the county of Albert, through about fifteen miles of the county of Westmoreland and thence through the county of King's to the city of St. John. It is not an ideal union for this reason : In the province of New Brunswick the nomination proceedings are always of interest to the electors. I do not know what the habit is in other sections of the Dominion but I do know that in New Brunswick it is the ambition of all the electors who can possibly do so to attend the nomination proceedings. The union of these three counties will make it almost impossible for the electors of Albert to attend the nomination because the county of King's, being the larger and more important one as far as population is concerned, will naturally swing the nomination and that will be held at the shirej town, which is Hampton, about twenty-two miles from St. John. Therefore, this will prevent the people of Albert from taking part in the nomination proceedings. I quite agree with the statement of the hon. member for| King's to the effect that this union is not) agreeable to the people of Albert, or to a very great many of them, those who consulted with me in respect to the matter at least! Nor, do I think that it is agreeable to the people of King's, but it seems to be inevitable. I recognize that if you were to take any two constituencies and unite them, that it "would give dissatisfaction, especially to the more populous constituency. It would be impossible to unite the constituencies of Restigouche and Gloucester, because they are growing constituencies, and tire unit would be very much larger than the unit of King's and Albert. As you cannot very well unite the county of St. John and the county of Albert, and as you cannot very well unite the counties of Gloucester and Restigouche, the proposed arrangement is the best that can be made, if you adhere to county boundaries. If you do not adhere to county boundaries, then it would seem to me that the county of St. John should be divided, the eastern portion of it attached to the county of King's, and the western' portion to the county of Charlotte. I do not think that arrangement would be satisfactory. It appears to me that under the circumstances, the proposed arrangement follows the line of least resistance, and having regard to the principle of county boundaries, I certainly would not move an amendment.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: From the point of view of community of interest, the union of Restigouche and Gloucester would be unobjectionable. The only point against that union would be that the population is increasing more rapidly in these counties than in the counties of Albert and King's.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
There is another objection. The county of Gloucester has two Mr. EMMERSON.
large islands which are removed from the mainland, and that would make it very much more inconvenient.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: How could that possibly be ? So far as the relation of the islands to the mainlands of Gloucester is concerned, that inconvenience already exists, and how could it be any worse if you added the county of Restigouche ? These two counties lie for their whole length beside each other. Their main roads are connected, and there is a constant interchange of trade between the people of both counties. The difficulty there is that the population of these united counties would be about 4,000 larger than the population of Albert and King's. However, that difference has not stood in the way in Nova Scotia and other provinces, and I do not see why it should be considered here. Another way to get rid of the difficulty is to have one member for the city and county of St. John.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: That would no doubt afford a solution.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: That is the proper solution of the difficulty, and I am sure it would please the member for Westmoreland. It certainly would please the people of Albert and King's, and every o*e in New Brunswick, except perhaps the member for St. John.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
We hope that next census we will have to add some memj bers to New Brunswick and not to subtract from its representation.
Schedule for New Brunswick agreed to.
On section 1,

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I desire to move that the following be added to the Bill as clause 1.	:
This Act may be cited as the Representation Act. 1903.	v

Motion agreed to.
On section 4,	:

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I move that the following be added as section 4 (a) :
Whenever in the said Bill, a municipality or place is wrongly referred to as a city or a town or a village, but there is within the territorial limits of the electoral district in the description to which the reference refers, a municipality or place, the same name as the city or town or village, but is not of the class of a city, town, or village, as the case may be specified in the schedule ; the reference shall be taken to be that municipality or place.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: It would be better to see that we are right in the first instance than to add this clause, but I suppose there are so many places mentioned that we cannot be certain.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Take for instance the village of Preston. I took that

from the Ontario Revised Statutes, but I find that a change has taken place recently and Preston is now a town. This clause would cover any possible chance of mistake.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I will now move that the committee rise ; report progress, and ask leave to sit again. This leaves for consideration clauses 36, 37 and 50 of the schedule which refers to the counties of Grey, Hastings and Waterloo. Of course, I need not say that if my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) has any objection to the changes which have been made in Quebec, we shall give him the facility of being heard.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Some communication was made to me privately by my hon. friend from West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) with regard to some slight change which he thought would be desirable in the boundaries of one of the constituencies in the North-west Territories. I was not able to assent to it, because I was not familiar with the conditions to which he referred. For what length of time will the Bill stand ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Till we have disposed of the National Transcontinental Railway Bill.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Then there will be ample time for me to have a consultation with the hon. gentleman before the committee meets again.
Progress reported.

maintopic: JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.

speechtext:
House went into committee to consider the following resolution :
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Act respecting the Judges of Provincial Courts, and to provide for an additioaal Judge of the Superior Court of Quebec, at a salary of $4,000 per annum.-The Minster of Justice.

maintopic: JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.
speechtext: Would my hon. friend the Minister of Justice he good enough to explain ?

maintopic: JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.
speechtext: I think I shall have to ask the committee to rise, because I find that I have not the draft of the Bill which I intend to base on this resolution. It is intended to provide for the appointment of an additional Superior Court judge in the province of Quebec for the district of Pontiac. Provision was made by the legislature of Quebec eight years ago for the appointment of this judge, hut effect was not given to it, because we 'did not think the business justified the making of the appointment. The district of Pontiac will be taken from the district of Hull, and will be constituted into a separate district. If there is any information which my hon. friend desires, I will procure it for him ; but this is simply giving effect to that legislation.
speakername: The MINISTER OF JUSTICE (Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick).

maintopic: JUDGES OF PROVINCIAL COURTS.
speechtext:
None of the members of the bar from the province of
Quebec' are here, and I am not at all familiar with the matter ; but I have no doubt that any information we desire can be obtained on the first or the second reading of the Bill, and therefore, I will not ask that there should be any delay to-night ; assuming, of course, that we can have the same discussion on the Bill that we might have had on tliis resolution.
Resolution reported, and read the first time.

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.

speechtext: The PRIME MINISTER moved the adjournment of the House.

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext: I understand that we are to take up the National Transcontinental Railway Bill on Monday ?

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext: Has the right hon. gentleman any information to give us to when the Bill with reference to the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act will he taken up ?

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext: Our intention is, as soon as we dispose of the National Transcontinental Railway Bill, to complete the Redistribution Bill, and then, I suppose, we will take up the other.

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext: My hon. friend the Minister of Finance will hear in mind that he was to lay on the Table of the House some documents with reference to that Bill.

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT-BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.
speechtext: At my hon. friend's suggestion, I will have the papers submitted in printed form, and the Bill will not be proceeded with until the papers are on the Table.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 11.50 p.m.
Monday, September 21, 1903.
